# Positivity of generalized cluster scattering diagrams

**Authors:** Amanda Burcroff Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: aburcroff@math.harvard.edu , Kyungyong Lee Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487, USA and Korea Institute for Advanced Study, Seoul 02455, Republic of Korea Email address: kyungyong.lee@ua.edu & klee1@kias.re.kr and Lang Mou Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Cologne, 50923 Köln, Germany Email address: langmou@math.uni-koeln.de

## Abstract

We introduce a new class of combinatorial objects, named tight gradings, which are certain nonnegative integer-valued functions on maximal Dyck paths. Using tight gradings, we derive a manifestly positive formula for any wall-function in a rank-2 generalized cluster scattering diagram. We further prove that any consistent rank-2 scattering diagram is positive with respect to the coefficients of initial wall-functions. Moreover, our formula yields explicit expressions for relative Gromov–Witten invariants on weighted projective planes and the Euler characteristics of moduli spaces of framed stable representations on complete bipartite quivers. Finally, by leveraging the rank-2 positivity, we show that any higher-rank generalized cluster scattering diagram has positive wall-functions, which leads to a proof of the positivity of the Laurent phenomenon and the strong positivity of Chekhov–Shapiro’s generalized cluster algebras.

- 1 Introduction

- 2 Rank 2 scattering diagrams and theta functions

- 3 Greedy bases for rank-2 generalized cluster algebras

- 4 The generalized greedy basis equals the generalized theta basis

- 5 Shadowed gradings and tight gradings

- 6 Applications of the tight and shadowed grading formulas

## 1. Introduction

In Fomin–Zelevinsky’s cluster algebras [18], cluster variables are iteratively generated rational functions in $n$ algebraically independent variables that are proven to remain Laurent polynomials, a property known as the Laurent phenomenon [19]. It was conjectured originally in [18] that the non-trivial coefficients in these Laurent polynomials are positive integers. The positivity of the Laurent phenomenon turned out to be a deep property that has driven plentiful research employing wide range of techniques across combinatorics, representation theory and algebraic geometry including [42, 45, 41, 12]. In this paper, we obtain new positivity results for the generalized cluster algebras of Chekhov and Shapiro [9] where polynomial type exchange relations (as opposed to binomials) are used to generate cluster variables. Our proofs are built upon a novel counting formula for wall-functions to rank-2 generalized cluster scattering diagrams and the subsequent positivity of wall-functions in higher ranks.

Lee and Schiffler [38] first proved the positivity for all skew-symmetric cluster algebras. Their proof is of an algebraic combinatorial nature and uses an explicit rank-2 formula of cluster variables in terms of combinatorics on Dyck paths [37]. This breakthrough led to Lee–Li–Zelevinsky’s construction of greedy bases of all rank-2 cluster algebras [36] and the subsequent generalization by Rupel [51]. Cluster monomials, which are monomials of cluster variables in one cluster, form only a proper subset of the greedy basis except for finite-type cases. So it is a significant feature of greedy bases that they give explicit combinatorial information even outside the discrete cluster dynamics.

In their seminal work [27], Gross, Hacking, Keel, and Konstevich solved a number of conjectures fundamental to the structures of cluster algebras by bringing in novel techniques from log Calabi–Yau mirror symmetry [26]. Scattering diagrams [31, 30], also known as wall-crossing structures, play a crucial role in this study. In particular, the authors constructed theta functions through cluster scattering diagrams and showed that the theta functions include all cluster monomials. The positivity of the Laurent phenomenon follows from the positivity of wall-functions in cluster scattering diagrams.

A main theme of [27] is to address Fock–Goncharov’s cluster duality [16, 17], in which it was conjectured that the algebra of functions on a cluster variety $V$ has a canonical basis containing global monomials parametrized by the tropical points $V^{\vee}(\mathbb{Z}^{T})$ of the mirror cluster variety $V^{\vee}$ . Although this conjecture is false in general [25], theta functions do serve as a topological basis that exists in a certain formal limit. For $V$ an $\mathcal{A}$ -type cluster variety, global monomials are precisely cluster monomials and they are parametrized by the tropical points inside the cluster complex $\Delta^{+}$ , which can be realized as a simplicial cone complex in the ambient real vector space of a cluster scattering diagram. The cluster complex $\Delta^{+}$ is usually infinite but not complete. As noted in [27], it is precisely the rich structure outside $\Delta^{+}$ that scattering diagram technique brings into the the cluster algebra picture.

Our discoveries stem from an effort to bridge the explicit combinatorial terms developed in [37, 38, 36, 51] and the more abstract constructions of [27] through scattering diagrams. Such a precedent is that greedy bases and theta bases are actually the same in rank 2 [10]. However, the explicit scattering diagram structure outside $\Delta^{+}$ is still elusive, even in rank 2. While one expects a non-trivial wall in every rational direction to appear in this region (Appendix B), the wall-function in general is notoriously hard to compute. Our formula presented in Theorem 1.2 computes any such wall-function in terms of combinatorics on Dyck paths. In fact, the formula itself is far more general than the ordinary cluster situation. As explained in Section 1.1, the formula essentially computes the commutator of two arbitrary generators of the tropical vertex group [31, 29]. As rank-2 scattering diagrams are already linked with other interesting objects [29, 49], our formula invites immediate applications to Gromov–Witten invariants and quiver representations; see Section 6.

An immediate consequence of Theorem 1.2 is that any wall-function has nonnegative integer coefficients. We extend this positivity to wall-functions in any rank-2 consistent scattering diagram (Theorem 1.4) and in any higher-rank generalized cluster scattering diagram (Theorem 1.5). The latter scattering diagrams encode structures of the associated generalized cluster algebras [40, 11]. The positivity of wall-functions allows us to prove the positivity of the Laurent phenomenon for any generalized cluster algebra, previously conjectured by Chekhov and Shapiro [9, Section 5]. The strong positivity, which says that the structure constants in the multiplication of theta functions are nonnegative, also follows.

We now give more detailed description of the main results in Section 1.1 through 1.3.

### 1.1. Formula for wall-functions

Let $\Bbbk$ be a field of characteristic zero. Following [29], we consider the automorphism group

$$ A\coloneqq\operatorname{Aut}_{\Bbbk\llbracket t\rrbracket}(\Bbbk[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}]\llbracket t\rrbracket) $$

of the $1$ -parameter formal family of the two-dimensional torus. For a non-zero vector $(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ and a function $f\in\Bbbk[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}]\llbracket t\rrbracket$ of the form

$$ f=1+tx^{a}y^{b}\cdot g(x^{a}y^{b},t),\quad g(z,t)\in\Bbbk[z]\llbracket t\rrbracket, $$

we define $T_{(a,b),f}\in A$ by

$$ T_{(a,b),f}(x)=f^{-b}\cdot x\quad\text{and}\quad T_{(a,b),f}(y)=f^{a}\cdot y. $$

Clearly $T_{(a,b),f}^{-1}=T_{(a,b),f^{-1}}\in A$ .

The tropical vertex group is the completion with respect to the maximal ideal $(t)\subseteq\Bbbk\llbracket t\rrbracket$ of the subgroup of $A$ generated by all elements of the form $T_{(a,b),f}$ . This group and its close variants arose in mirror symmetry [31, 30], and subsequently also play important roles in wall-crossing identities of invariants in triangulated categories [32, 33].

One initial task to understand the tropical vertex group is to compute the ordered factorization of the commutator of two generators. This turns out to be a rather hard question, but investigations into it have led to links to interesting objects including relative Gromov–Witten invariants [29, 28] and moduli spaces of stable quiver representations [47, 48, 49]. Our approach to this problem is combinatorial and is largely motivated by Fomin–Zelevinsky’s cluster structure.

Let $P_{1}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{1,k}x^{k}$ and $P_{2}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{2,k}y^{k}$ be elements in $\Bbbk[x^{\pm 1},y^{\pm 1}]\llbracket t\rrbracket$ . Here $p_{i,k}\in\Bbbk\llbracket t\rrbracket$ , $i=1,2$ are regarded as coefficients. As observed by Kontsevich and Soibelman [31], there exists a unique ordered factorization of the commutator

$$ T_{(0,1),P_{2}}^{-1}\cdot T_{(1,0),P_{1}}\cdot T_{(0,1),P_{2}}\cdot T_{(1,0),P_{1}}^{-1}=\prod_{b/a\ \text{decreasing}}^{\rightarrow}T_{(a,b),f_{(a,b)}}. $$

The right-hand side of (1.1) is an infinite product ranging over all positive coprime pairs $(a,b)$ . It is understood as the limit of finite products modulo each $(t^{n})$ for $n\geq 1$ .

#### Theorem 1.2 (Tight grading formula).

Fix coprime positive integers $(a,b)$ . For each $k\geq 1$ , choose integers $(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ such that $ad_{2,k}-bd_{1,k}=\pm 1$ , $ka\leq d_{1,k}$ , and $kb\leq d_{2,k}$ . Then

$$ f_{(a,b)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\omega}\mathrm{wt}(\omega)x^{ka}y^{kb}, $$

where the second sum is over all tight gradings $\omega$ on the Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ of total horizontal weight $kb$ and total vertical weight $ka$ , and $\mathrm{wt}(\omega)\in\Bbbk\llbracket t\rrbracket$ is the weight monomial in $\{p_{i,k}\mid i=1,2,k\geq 1\}$ associated to $\omega$ .

Tight gradings, the main combinatorial ingredients in Theorem 1.2, have simple descriptions in terms of combinatorics on the Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ given in Section 3.2 and Section 5.1. They form a subset of Rupel’s compatible gradings [51], whose definition was inspired by the compatible pairs defined by Lee–Li–Zelevinsky in [36]. The formula (1.3) was announced in [7, Theorem 3.5] with a proof sketch. We give two different proofs in Section 5.4 and Section 5.5.

Theorem 1.2 is a special case of Theorem 5.17, where we give a combinatorial formula of the $m$ -th power of $f_{(a,b)}$ for any $m\geq 1$ using more general shadowed gradings. The more general formula will be used to compute Euler characteristics of quiver moduli spaces; see Corollary 6.3. It also yields explicit expressions of relative Gromov–Witten invariants on weighted projective planes; see Theorem 6.8.

We give in Theorem 9.5 a formula for the commutator of two arbitrary generators $T_{(a_{1},b_{1}),f_{1}}$ and $T_{(a_{2},b_{2}),f_{2}}$ in the tropical vertex group. The difference with Theorem 1.2 is that the vectors $(a_{1},b_{1})$ and $(a_{2},b_{2})$ may only generate a proper rank-2 sub-lattice of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . One may compare this formula with Gross–Pandharipande–Siebert’s full commutator formula [29, Section 5], which involves relative Gromov–Witten invariants defined through orbifold blowups of toric surfaces and a process factorizing $f_{1},f_{2}$ into products of binomials. Our formula is direct in terms of the coefficients of $f_{1},f_{2}$ and by counting combinatorial objects. It is thus much simpler from the perspective of computation and can be efficiently implemented through computer programs.

### 1.2. Positivity of scattering diagrams

In the main body of the paper, the factorization (1.1) is packed in a structure called a rank-2 consistent scattering diagram determined by two initial lines. More generally such a structure $\mathfrak{D}=\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})$ can start with a countable collection $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ of lines in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and result in adding a collection $\mathfrak{D}\cut\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ of rays in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to achieve consistency. Lines and rays are uniformly called walls and are attached with wall-functions. Each $f_{(a,b)}$ in (1.1) is the wall-function associated to the ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ while $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are associated to the coordinate axes. We will soon see this description in Section 2.2.

The starting point of the remaining discussion is the positivity demonstrated by the tight grading formula (1.3). The combined coefficient for each term $x^{ka}y^{kb}$ is a polynomial with nonnegative integer coefficients, that is, an element in

$$ \mathbb{N}[p_{i,k}\mid i=1,2,k\geq 1], $$

where $\mathbb{N}$ denotes $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ throughout. It turns out that this positivity is shared by any consistent scattering diagram in rank 2.

#### Theorem 1.4 (Theorem 9.9).

Let $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ be an initial scattering diagram consisting of lines. Any coefficient of any wall-function in $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})$ can be expressed as a polynomial in the coefficients of wall-functions in $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients.

We next utilize Theorem 1.4 to show the positivity of wall-functions of certain scattering diagrams living in higher dimensions. There will be immediate implications on several positivity phenomena of generalized cluster algebras.

Briefly, a scattering diagram in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ is a (countable) collection of codimension one rational polyhedral cones, each with an attached power series, referred to as walls and their wall-functions. The (ordinary) cluster scattering diagram of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich [27] is determined by a finite collection of initial walls through a higher dimensional consistency condition that generalizes the equation (1.1). These scattering diagrams encode the information of Fomin–Zelevinsky’s cluster algebras.

In more concrete terms, a generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is the unique consistent completion of an initial collection of walls

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s},\mathrm{in}}=\{(H_{i},f_{i})\mid i=1,\dots,n\} $$

such that $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}\cut\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s},\mathrm{in}}$ consists only of non-incoming walls, a notion in higher dimensions generalizing rays in rank 2. Each $H_{i}$ is the coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ (for $n\leq N$ ) with vanishing $i$ -th coordinate and

$$ f_{i}=1+p_{i,1}x^{w_{i}}+\dots+p_{i,\ell_{i}}x^{\ell_{i}w_{i}}, $$

where each $w_{i}$ is a (column) vector in $\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ , $\ell_{i}$ is a positive integer, and $p_{i,k}$ are formal variables. The matrix $(\ell_{1}w_{1},\dots,\ell_{n}w_{n})$ is assumed to have full rank. Its top $n\times n$ submatrix needs to be skew-symmetrizable, as required for exchange matrices that govern mutations in cluster algebras. These scattering diagrams, constructed and studied in [40, 11], generalize the cluster scattering diagrams of [27], where each $P_{i}$ is a binomial $1+x^{\ell_{i}w_{i}}$ . They encode the information of Chekhov–Shapiro’s generalized cluster algebras [9].

A significant property of ordinary cluster scattering diagrams is the positivity of wall-functions [27, Theorem 1.24], which says that any wall-function is a (possibly infinite) product of binomials of the form $(1+x^{w})$ . Thus, as a power series, every wall-function has nonnegative integer coefficients. The proof in loc. cit heavily relies on the assumption that the initial wall-functions are binomials. Our next main result shows the positivity of wall-functions in the polynomial case.

#### Theorem 1.5 (Theorem 8.11).

Any wall-function in a generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ has coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[p_{i,s}\mid 1\leq i\leq n,1\leq s\leq\ell_{i}]$ .

The proof of Theorem 1.5 relies on Theorem 1.4, the rank-2 positivity in full generality. In Section 9.3, we give an order-by-order construction of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ analogous to the algorithm in [27, Appendix C], where local scatterings are essentially governed by rank-2 behaviors. Then the proof undergoes a careful induction that ensures positivity at each order.

#### Remark 1.6.

It would be interesting to explore quiver representation-theoretic interpretations of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ beyond the rank-2 case (Section 6.1). Following Bridgeland [4], stability scattering diagrams equivalent to a particular class of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ are constructed in [35] through representations of Jacobian algebras whose quivers have loops. Theorem 1.5 then implies that the Euler characteristic type wall-function coefficients in [35] are all nonnegative integers.

### 1.3. Positivity of generalized cluster algebras

The remaining structural properties regarding the positivity of generalized cluster algebras follow from Theorem 1.5, summarized below. This is a series of results extended from the ordinary case [27].

#### Theorem 1.7.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ (resp. $\mathcal{U}$ ) denote the generalized cluster algebra (resp. upper cluster algebra) associated to a generalized cluster structure (with coefficients and frozen directions) of Chekhov–Shapiro as defined in Section 7.

- (1) Every cluster monomial in $\mathcal{A}$ is a Laurent polynomial in the cluster variables of any cluster with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}]$ where $\mathbb{P}$ is the coefficient group. (Theorem 7.9)

- (2) When the cluster structure is generated by a seed data $\mathbf{s}$ (Section 8.1) that determines $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ , we have the so-called theta functions $\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}\}$ constructed from $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ in certain formal completion $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ (dependent on $\mathbf{s}$ ) of $\mathcal{U}$ . Each $\vartheta_{m}$ is a formal Laurent series with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}]$ . The set of theta functions contain all cluster monomials. (Theorem 8.26)

- (3) Theta functions form a topological basis of $\,\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ and satisfy the formal multiplicative rule

$$ \vartheta_{p_{1}}\cdot\vartheta_{p_{2}}=\sum_{q\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};q)\vartheta_{q}\in\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}, $$

where each structure constant $\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ is defined through broken lines and is in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}]$ . (Theorem 8.30)

- (4) The $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -module

$$ \mathcal{M}\coloneqq\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]}\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in\mathbb{Z}^{N},\vartheta_{m}\in\mathcal{U}\} $$

is closed under multiplication, hence a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -algebra. There are natural inclusions $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{U}$ . (Theorem 8.34)

- (5) Theta functions are characterized as the atomic elements in $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ with respect to the scattering atlas. (Theorem 8.37)

Theorem 1.7(1) confirms the positivity of the Laurent phenomenon for generalized cluster algebras, previously conjectured by Chekhov and Shapiro [9]. It is proven in Section 8.3 through Theorem 1.7(2). We refer to Theorem 1.7(3) as the strong positivity. There is an extensive discussion in [27] on when any of the inclusions $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{U}$ in the ordinary case becomes equality, which we expect to naturally carry over to the generalized case but do not discuss in this paper. Theorem 1.7(5) is suggested to the authors by Ben Davison. The proof follows Mandel’s [39] in the ordinary case.

### 1.4. Structure of the paper

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review rank-2 scattering diagrams and important constructions such as broken lines and theta functions. Generalized cluster scattering diagrams in rank 2 are studied in detail in Section 2.2, whose cluster complex structure leads to the definition of rank-2 generalized cluster algebras in Section 2.3.

In Section 3.1, we define greedy elements for rank-2 generalized cluster algebras through a positive recurrence of coefficients. Compatible gradings are defined in Section 3.2 and are used to express greedy elements in Section 3.3.

We establish the equality between greedy elements and theta functions in Section 4, generalizing [10]. This serves as a main ingredient in our first proof of Theorem 5.17 given in Section 5.4.

In Section 5, we introduce the main combinatorial objects shadowed gradings and tight gradings and prove Theorem 5.17, which is a more general formula covering Theorem 1.2. Definitions and examples of shadowed and tight gradings are given in Section 5.1. Another important ingredient towards Theorem 5.17 is the one-bending property regarding combinatorics of broken lines, introduced in Section 5.2. Two different proofs for Theorem 5.17 are given respectively in Sections 5.4 and 5.5.

In Section 6, we apply Theorem 5.17 to obtain combinatorial formulas for Euler characteristics of quiver moduli spaces and relative Gromov–Witten invariants.

Sections 7 and 8 deal with positivity properties of generalized cluster algebras. We review Chekhov–Shapiro’s generalized cluster structure in Section 7 and state the positivity of Laurent phenomenon in Theorem 7.9, whose proof is given in Section 8.3. Generalized cluster scattering diagrams are defined in Section 8.1. The cluster complex structure is described in Section 8.2. Other structural results regarding generalized cluster algebras such as the strong positivity and atomicity of theta functions are discussed in Sections 8.4 and 8.5.

In Section 9, we fill in rather technical results on positivity of scattering diagrams. We establish the full positivity in rank 2 in Sections 9.1 and 9.2. The proof of Theorem 8.11, the positivity of higher-rank generalized cluster scattering diagrams, is completed in Section 9.3.

Appendix A contains the proof of the compatible grading formula for greedy elements in generalized cluster algebras. In Appendix B, we give a combinatorial proof that the Badlands wall-function coefficients are non-vanishing in rank- $2$ generalized cluster scattering diagrams whose initial wall-functions have positive coefficients.
