### 5.2. One-bending property

The bend-type of a broken line is the tuple $(r(m_{0}),\dots,r(m_{\ell}))\in M^{\ell+1}$ . In a scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ , for a fixed endpoint $Q$ , every broken line $\beta$ with a given bend-type has identical image in $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ . This can be seen by working backwards from $Q$ to reconstruct the broken line.

Consider a generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}=\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ .

#### Definition 5.9.

Let $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ and coprime $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ such that

$$ d_{1}b-d_{2}a\neq 0. $$

Let $\beta$ be a (possible) broken line in $\mathfrak{D}$ such that it has initial exponent $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ , one unique bend at the wall $(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b),f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)})$ , and final exponent $(ka-d_{1},kb-d_{2})$ for $k\geq 1$ . We say that the pair $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfies the one-bending property (with respect to $\mathfrak{D}$ ) if any broken line that

$$ (-d_{1},-d_{2}) (-d_{1}+ka,-d_{2}+kb) $$

has the same bend-type as $\beta$ .

#### Remark 5.12.

Let $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property. Depending on the choice of terminal point $Q\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ , there is either exactly one broken line or no broken lines satisfying (5.10) and (5.11) and terminating at $Q$ . In particular, there will be one such broken line if

$$ Q\in\begin{cases}\left\{(q_{1},q_{2})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}:q_{2}<\min\left(\frac{kb-d_{2}}{ka-d_{1}}q_{1},\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}q_{1}\right)\right\}&\text{ if }d_{1}b-d_{2}a>0,\\[10.0pt]
\left\{(q_{1},q_{2})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}:q_{2}>\max\left(\frac{kb-d_{2}}{ka-d_{1}}q_{1},\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}q_{1}\right)\right\}&\text{ if }d_{1}b-d_{2}a<0,\end{cases} $$

and no such broken lines otherwise.

#### Lemma 5.13.

If $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy

$$ \frac{kab+1}{kb^{2}}\geq\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}>\frac{a}{b}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{ka^{2}}{kab+1}\leq\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}<\frac{a}{b}, $$

then they satisfy the one-bending property.

#### Proof.

We prove for the first case and the second case is similar. It suffices to show that there is no broken line satisfying (5.10) and (5.11) that bends at least twice. Suppose that there is one such $\beta$ . Notice that $\beta$ can only bend at walls strictly below $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d_{1},d_{2})$ , that is, walls $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a^{\prime},b^{\prime})$ such that

$$ \frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}>\frac{a^{\prime}}{b^{\prime}}. $$

Denote the amount of bending cumulated between $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ (inclusive) by $(a_{1},b_{1})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ . Denote the amount of bending cumulated between $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ (exclusive) and $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(0,1)$ (inclusive) by $(a_{2},b_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ . Thus $(a_{1},b_{1})+(a_{2},b_{2})=(ka,kb)$ . Now we have

$$ \frac{kab+1}{kb^{2}}\geq\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}>\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}>\frac{a}{b}>\frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}. $$

We note that since $\beta$ bends at least twice, the last three inequalities are all strict. We derive from $\dfrac{kab+1}{kb^{2}}>\dfrac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}>\dfrac{a}{b}$ and $b_{1}\leq kb$ that

$$ ab_{1}+\frac{b_{1}}{kb}>a_{1}b>ab_{1}\implies ab_{1}+1>a_{1}b>ab_{1}. $$

There is no integer solution for $(a_{1},b_{1})$ and hence such a broken line $\beta$ does not exist. ∎

#### Corollary 5.14.

Let $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ be coprime and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ .

- (1) If $(d_{1},d_{2})=(kab+1,kb^{2})$ or $(ka^{2},kab+1)$ , then $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property.

- (2) If $d_{1}\geq mka$ when $d_{1}b-d_{2}a<0$ or $d_{2}\geq mkb$ when $d_{1}b-d_{2}a>0$ where $m=|d_{1}b-d_{2}a|$ , then $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property.

- (3) For any $m>0$ , there exist infinitely many $(d_{1},d_{2})$ such that $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property and that $m=|d_{1}b-d_{2}a|$ .

#### Proof.

Statement (1) is a direct corollary of Lemma 5.13. We prove (2) when $m=d_{1}b-d_{2}a$ , and the other case is similar. Again by Lemma 5.13, it suffices to check

$$ \frac{kab+1}{kb^{2}}=\frac{a}{b}+\frac{1}{kb^{2}}\geq\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\iff\frac{1}{kb^{2}}\geq\frac{m}{d_{2}b}\iff d_{2}\geq mkb. $$

For (3), choose some $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ so that $m=|d_{1}b-d_{2}a|$ . By (2), for sufficiently large $N$ , $(d_{1}+Na,d_{2}+Nb)$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property. ∎

Consider the ordinary cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})}=\Scat(1+x^{\ell_{1}},1+y^{\ell_{2}})$ . More one-bending pairs can be found and will be useful in later applications. Notice that in this case, the total amount of bending of a broken line can only be of the form $(k\ell_{1}\bar{a},k\ell_{2}\bar{b})$ , where $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $(\bar{a},\bar{b})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ is coprime.

#### Lemma 5.15.

Let $(\bar{a},\bar{b})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ be coprime and $k\geq 1$ .

- (1) If $\bar{b}\leq\ell_{1}$ , then the vectors $(d_{1},d_{2})=(k\ell_{1}\bar{a}+1,k\ell_{2}\bar{b})$ and $(k\ell_{1}\bar{a},k\ell_{2}\bar{b})$ satisfy the one-bending property with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})}$ .

- (2) If $\bar{a}\leq\ell_{2}$ , then the vectors $(d_{1},d_{2})=(k\ell_{1}\bar{a},k\ell_{2}\bar{b}+1)$ and $(k\ell_{1}\bar{a},k\ell_{2}\bar{b})$ satisfy the one-bending property with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove (1) and the other case is similar. As in the proof of Lemma 5.13, it suffices to show that there is no integer solution $a_{1}\leq k\bar{a}$ , $b_{1}\leq k\bar{b}$ for the inequality

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k\ell_{1}\bar{a}+1}{k\ell_{2}\bar{b}}>\frac{\ell_{1}a_{1}}{\ell_{2}b_{1}}>\frac{\ell_{1}\bar{a}}{\ell_{2}\bar{b}}\quad\iff\quad b_{1}\bar{a}+\frac{b_{1}}{k\ell_{1}}>a_{1}\bar{b}>b_{1}\bar{a}. $$

Since $b_{1}\leq k\bar{b}\leq k\ell_{1}$ , we have that $a_{1}\bar{b}$ belongs to an open interval without any integer in it. ∎

The above lemma applies in particular to the central ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(\ell_{1}\bar{a},\ell_{2}\bar{b})$ with $(\bar{a},\bar{b})=(1,1)$ .

### 5.3. Formula for wall-functions

Fix two positive integers $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ . Consider the generalized cluster scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}=\Scat\left(1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{1}}p_{1,k}x^{k},1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{2}}p_{2,k}y^{k}\right). $$

Let $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ be coprime. Let $m$ be a positive integer. Then we can express the $m$ -th power of the wall-function $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ by

$$ \left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{m}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)x^{ka}y^{kb}, $$

where each coefficient $\lambda^{(m)}(a,b)$ is a polynomial in $\{p_{i,j}\mid i=1,2,1\leq j\leq\ell_{i}\}$ . When $m=1$ , we simply denote $\lambda(ka,kb)=\lambda^{(1)}(ka,kb)$ .

#### Theorem 5.17 (Shadowed grading formula).

$$ \left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{m}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\omega}\mathrm{wt}(\omega)x^{ka}y^{kb}, $$

where the second sum is over all shadowed gradings on the Dyck path $\mathcal{P}(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ of total horizontal weight $kb$ and total vertical weight $ka$ for any $(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ such that

- • $d_{1,k}\geq ka$ and $d_{2,k}\geq kb$ ,

- • $(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property,

- • $m=|ad_{2,k}-bd_{1,k}|$ .

For any tuple $\mathbf{Q}=(q_{j})_{j=1}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{N}^{\ell}$ , define the weighted sum $w(\mathbf{Q})\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}jq_{j}$ . For tuples $\mathbf{Q}_{i}=(q_{i,j})_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}\in\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{i}}$ , $i=1,2$ , denote $p_{i}^{\mathbf{Q}_{i}}=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,j}^{q_{i,j}}$ . Then the expression (5.16) can be refined as

$$ \left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{m}=\sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb\end{subarray}}\lambda^{(m)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}. $$

It follows from Theorem 5.17 that for each $(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ such that $w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka,w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb$ ,

$$ \lambda^{(m)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})=\left|\left\{\omega\,\middle|\,\text{$\omega$ is shadowed},\ \mathrm{wt}(\omega)=p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}\right\}\right|, $$

that is, the number of shadowed gradings on $\mathcal{P}(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ whose weight polynomial is $p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}$ . The fact that this number computes $\lambda_{a,b}^{(m)}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ implies it does not depend on the choice of $(d_{1,k},d_{2,k})$ . This turns out to be a rather delicate property of shadowed gradings from the view of combinatorics.

#### Remark 5.20.

When $m=1$ , any $d_{1,k}\geq ka$ , $d_{2,k}\geq kb$ such that $|ad_{2,k}-bd_{2,k}|=1$ satisfy the one-bending property by Corollary 5.14(2). In this case, shadowed gradings are precisely tight gradings and the formula (5.18) was announced in [7, Theorem 3.5].

We can use the formula (5.18) to directly calculate the wall-function of the single wall comprising the Badlands in an affine cluster scattering diagram.

#### Example 5.21.

Consider the cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{(2,2)}$ . It follows from Theorem 5.17 and Example 5.7 that

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,1)}=\sum_{k\geq 0}(k+1)x^{2k}y^{2k}\,. $$

This was known to experts [32] and was shown using quiver representations by Reineke [47].

#### Example 5.22.

Consider the cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{(4,1)}$ . It follows from Theorem 5.17 and Example 5.8 that

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,1)}=\sum_{k\geq 0}(2k+1)x^{4k}y^{2k}\,. $$

This has been previously calculated by Reading [46] using limits of $F$ -polynomial expressions.

### 5.4. Proof of Theorem 5.17

We now prove the shadowed grading formula for the coefficients of powers of wall-functions, as described in Section 5.3. This proof relies on the fact that the generalized greedy and generalized theta bases coincide, a result established in Section 4. We use the one-bending property from Section 5.2 to refine the equality of these bases, allowing us to find the shadowed gradings corresponding to a particularly nice broken line. This broken line is chosen to have weight equal to a chosen coefficient of the power of a wall-function, yielding the desired formula in terms of shadowed gradings.

For the entirety of this subsection, fix $a$ , $b$ , $k$ , and $m$ as in Section 5.3, and set $d_{1}\coloneqq d_{1,k}$ and $d_{2}\coloneqq d_{2,k}$ .

Recall that $\CG(p,q)$ is the set of compatible gradings $\omega$ on $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}([d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+})$ with $p=\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})$ and $q=\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})$ . We let $\CG_{+}^{t}(p,q)\subseteq\CG(p,q)$ consist of the compatible gradings with $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}\cut\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}))=t$ . Similarly, we let $\CG_{-}^{t}(p,q)\subseteq\CG(p,q)$ consist of the gradings with $\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}\cut\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}))=t$ . Let

$$ \CG^{t}(p,q)=\begin{cases}\CG_{+}^{t}(p,q)&\text{ if $bd_{1}\geq ad_{2}$},\\
\CG_{-}^{t}(p,q)&\text{ otherwise,}\end{cases} $$

and let $|\CG^{t}(p,q)|=\sum_{\omega\in\CG^{t}(ka,kb)}\text{wt}(\omega)\in\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{M}]$ . We show in the following lemma that $\CG^{0}(p,q)$ is precisely the set of shadowed gradings in $\CG(p,q)$ .

#### Lemma 5.23.

One of $\CG^{0}_{\pm}(p,q)$ is empty unless $p=q=0$ . Precisely, when $(p,q)\neq(0,0)$ ,

- (1) $\CG^{0}_{+}(p,q)=\varnothing$ if $qd_{1}\leq pd_{2}$ ;

- (2) $\CG^{0}_{-}(p,q)=\varnothing$ if $qd_{1}\geq pd_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

By symmetry, it is enough to prove the first case, where we assume $\frac{q}{p}\leq\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}$ . Suppose such a compatible grading $\omega$ exists. By assumption, we have $\frac{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}{\omega(\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}))}=\frac{q}{p}$ . Hence there must be some horizontal edge $u$ such that $\frac{\omega(u)}{\omega(\sh(u))}\leq\frac{q}{p}$ . Choose $v$ to be the unique vertical edge such that $|(\overrightarrow{uv})_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega(u)$ .

By the compatibility of $\omega$ , we must have $|(\overrightarrow{uv})_{\mathbf{E}}|\geq\omega(\sh(u))+1$ . However, by the modular definition of the maximal Dyck path (see, for example, [2, Lemma 1.3]), we then must have that $\omega(\sh(u))d_{2}<\omega(u)d_{1}$ . However, this yields a contradiction since we have $\frac{\omega(u)}{\omega(\sh(u))}\leq\frac{q}{p}\leq\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}$ . ∎

Fix an endpoint $Q=(Q_{1},Q_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{>0}$ such that the quantity $(-m+ka)Q_{2}-(-n+kb)Q_{1}$ is positive if $bd_{1}\leq d_{2}a$ , and negative otherwise. Let $\BL(ka,kb)$ denote the set of broken lines with initial exponent $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ and final exponent $(-d_{1}+ka,-d_{2}+kb)$ that terminate at $Q$ . Let $\BL^{t}(ka,kb)$ denote the subset of broken lines in $\BL(ka,kb)$ that bend at the positive $y$ -axis with multiplicity $t$ . Given a set $B$ of broken lines, let $|B|\coloneqq\sum_{\beta\in B}c(\beta)$ .

#### Lemma 5.24.

For all $t\in\{0,1,\dots,kb\}$ , we have

$$ |\BL^{t}(ka,kb)|=|\CG^{t}(ka,kb)|\,. $$

#### Proof.

We handle the case when $bd_{1}\geq ad_{2}$ , with the other case following analogously. We proceed by induction on the quantity $kb-t$ . The base case $kb-t=0$ is readily checked, as both quantities are simply a product of two binomial coefficients.

For the inductive step, we first note that the sets $\CG(ka,kb-t)$ and $\BL(ka,kb-t)$ can be refined as $\CG(ka,kb-t)=\bigcup_{s=0}^{kb-t}\CG^{s}(ka,kb-t)$ and $\BL(ka,kb-t)=\bigcup_{s=0}^{kb-t}\BL^{s}(ka,kb-t)$ . Since these unions are disjoint, we have

$$ \displaystyle|\CG(ka,kb-t)| \displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{kb-t}|\CG^{s}(ka,kb-t)|, \displaystyle|\BL(ka,kb-t)| \displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{kb-t}|\BL^{s}(ka,kb-t)|\,. $$

Applying Theorem 4.1 yields

$$ \sum_{s=0}^{kb-t}|\CG^{s}(ka,kb-t)|=\sum_{s=0}^{kb-t}|\BL^{s}(ka,kb-t)|\,. $$

Using the inductive hypothesis, we have $|\CG^{s}(ka,kb-t)|=|\BL^{s}(ka,kb-t)|$ for $s>0$ . Hence we can also conclude $|\CG^{0}(ka,kb-t)|=|\BL^{0}(ka,kb-t)|$ . By separating out the contribution of the edges in $\mathcal{P}_{N}\cut\sh(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})$ to the weight of each compatible grading, we see

$$ |\CG^{t}(ka,kb)|=\pi_{d_{1}-ka,t}(p_{2,\bullet})|\CG^{0}(ka,kb-t)|\,. $$

We also have

$$ |\BL^{t}(ka,kb)|=\pi_{d_{1}-ka,t}(p_{2,\bullet})|\BL^{0}(ka,kb-t)|\,, $$

which can be seen examining the preimage of the map taking each broken line in $\BL^{t}(ka,kb)$ to a broken line in $\BL^{0}(ka,kb-t)$ by forgetting the last bending. We can therefore conclude $|\BL^{t}(ka,kb)|=|\CG^{t}(ka,kb)|$ , as desired. ∎

#### Proposition 5.25.

We have $|\BL^{0}(ka,kb)|=\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)$ .

#### Proof.

It follows directly from Corollary 5.14(2) and Remark 5.12 (using our choice of $Q$ ) that $\BL^{0}(ka,kb)$ consists of a single broken line. This broken line, which we denote by $\beta$ , bends with multiplicity $k$ at the wall of slope $\frac{b}{a}$ with no other bendings. By hypothesis, we have $|(d_{1},d_{2})\cdot(-b,a)|=m$ . Thus, the weight associated to the bending of $\beta$ over $\mathfrak{d}$ with multiplicity $k$ is given by the coefficient of $x^{kb}y^{ka}$ in $(f_{\mathfrak{d}})^{m}$ , which is precisely $\lambda(ka,kb)$ . Since $\beta$ is the unique broken line in $\BL^{0}(ka,kb)$ and $\beta$ only bends once, we can conclude that $|\BL^{0}(ka,kb)|=|\beta|=\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)$ , as desired. ∎

#### Remark 5.26.

In the cluster algebra case, a tight grading has weight $1$ if it takes values in $\{0,\ell_{1}\}$ on the vertical edges and $\{0,\ell_{2}\}$ on the horizontal edges, and weight $0$ otherwise. If we restrict to considering only these gradings, then the total weight of gradings in $\CG^{t}(ka,kb)$ is the same as its cardinality. Thus, in order for $|\CG^{t}(ka,kb)|$ to be nonzero, $t$ must be a multiple of $\ell_{1}$ .

The first main theorem now readily follows.

#### Proof of Theorem 5.17.

By Lemma 5.23, the gradings in $\CG^{0}(ka,kb)$ are precisely the shadowed gradings contributing to the formula in Theorem 5.17. Hence the main result follows directly by combining the equalities in Lemma 5.24 and Proposition 5.25 when $t=0$ . ∎

### 5.5. Another proof of Theorem 5.17

We provide an alternative proof that does not rely on the results in Section 4.

We first prove some simple properties of shadowed gradings, allowing us to relate them to the the polynomials $d_{+}(p,q)$ and $d_{-}(p,q)$ .

#### Lemma 5.27.

We have

$$ \displaystyle|\CG(p,q)| \displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{p}\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})\left|\CG^{0}_{+}(p-s,q)\right| \displaystyle=\sum_{s=0}^{q}\pi_{d_{1}-p,s}(p_{2,\bullet})\left|\CG^{0}_{-}(p,q-s)\right|\,. $$

#### Proof.

The first equality follows by viewing $s$ as total value of $\omega$ on the horizontal edges outside of $\sh(S_{2})$ , so $|\CG(p,q)|=\sum_{s=0}^{p}|\CG^{s}_{+}(p-s,q)|$ . Each summand $\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})\left|\CG^{0}_{+}(p-s,q)\right|$ on the right hand side is then equal to $|\CG^{s}_{+}(p,q)|$ , where $\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})$ accounts for the weight contributed by the horizontal edges outside $\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}})$ and $|\CG^{0}_{+}(p-s,q)|$ accounts for the remaining weight of all vertical edges and the horizontal edges in $\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}})$ . The second equality follows similarly, reversing the roles of vertical and horizontal edges. ∎

#### Proposition 5.28.

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})$ . For any $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , we have

$$ |\CG_{+}^{0}(p,q)|=d_{+}(p,q)\quad\text{and}\quad|\CG_{-}^{0}(p,q)|=d_{-}(p,q). $$

#### Proof.

Recall $d_{\pm}(p,q)$ from Definition 3.7. We prove by induction on $(p,q)$ . The base case is

$$ |\CG_{+}^{0}(0,0)|=d_{+}(0,0)=1\quad\text{and}\quad|\CG_{-}^{0}(0,0)|=d_{-}(0,0)=1. $$

Then the result follows from Lemma 5.27, Lemma 3.8, and $|\CG(p,q)|=c(p,q)$ from Theorem 3.18. ∎

#### Corollary 5.29.

The polynomials $d_{\pm}(p,q)$ satisfy

$$ \sum_{s=0}^{p}\pi_{d_{2}-q,s}(p_{1,\bullet})d_{+}(p-s,q)=\sum_{s=0}^{q}\pi_{d_{1}-p,s}(p_{2,\bullet})d_{-}(p,q-s). $$

When $(p,q)\neq(0,0)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle d_{+}(p,q)=0\quad\text{when}\quad d_{1}q\leq d_{2}p; \displaystyle d_{-}(p,q)=0\quad\text{when}\quad d_{1}q\geq d_{2}p. $$

#### Proof.

This is a direct corollary of Lemma 5.23, Lemma 5.27, and Proposition 5.28. ∎

As a consequence of Proposition 5.28, we present the following sharpened recursive formula of $c(p,q)$ , which generalizes [36, Proposition 1.6] and [51, Proposition 2.13].

#### Proposition 5.30.

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ . The polynomials $c(p,q)$ satisfy the following recursion

$$ c(p,q)=\begin{cases}\sum_{k=1}^{p}-c(p-k,q)\varsigma_{d_{2}-q,k}(p_{1,\bullet})\quad&\text{if $d_{1}q\leq d_{2}p$;}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{q}-c(p,q-k)\varsigma_{d_{1}-p,k}(p_{2,\bullet})\quad&\text{if $d_{1}q\geq d_{2}p$.}\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

With the emphasis on $d_{\pm}(p,q)$ , the stated recursion of $c(p,q)$ follows immediately from Corollary 5.29 and Definition 3.7. We also see that $c(p,q)$ is attained by one of two polynomials in Definition 3.5. ∎

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ . Let $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let

$$ \BL^{t}_{+}(p,q)=\BL^{t}_{+}(d_{1},d_{2},p,q)\quad\text{(resp. $\BL^{t}_{-}(p,q)=\BL^{t}_{-}(d_{1},d_{2},p,q)$)} $$

denote the set of broken lines with initial exponent $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ , final exponent $(-d_{1}+p,-d_{2}+q)$ , and endpoint $Q_{+}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}$ (resp. $Q_{-}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}$ ) chosen close enough to the positive $x$ -axis (resp. positive $y$ -axis) such that the bend at the positive $x$ -axis (resp. positive $y$ -axis) corresponds to the monomial $x^{t}$ (resp. $y^{t}$ ).

#### Lemma 5.31.

We have

$$ \displaystyle|\BL_{+}^{t}(p,q)| \displaystyle=\pi_{d_{2}-q,t}(p_{1,\bullet})|\BL_{+}^{0}(p-t,q)|, \displaystyle|\BL_{-}^{t}(p,q)| \displaystyle=\pi_{d_{1}-p,t}(p_{2,\bullet})|\BL_{-}^{0}(p,q-t)|. $$

#### Proof.

When it is non-empty, erasing the last bending of any broken line in $\BL_{+}^{t}(p,q)$ (resp. $\BL_{-}^{t}(p,q)$ ) induces a surjection to $\BL_{+}^{0}(p-t,q)$ (resp. $\BL_{-}^{0}(p,q-t)$ ). The computation of the weights follows from the initial wall-functions on the axes.

If $\BL_{+}^{t}(p,q)$ is empty, then either $\pi_{d_{2}-q,t}(p_{1,\bullet})=0$ or $\BL_{+}^{0}(p-t,q)$ is empty. The same is true for the $-$ case. ∎

#### Lemma 5.32.

One of $\BL^{0}_{\pm}(p,q)$ is empty unless $p=q=0$ . Precisely, when $(p,q)\neq(0,0)$ ,

- (1) $\BL^{0}_{+}(p,q)=\varnothing$ if $qd_{1}\leq d_{2}p$ ,

- (2) $\BL^{0}_{-}(p,q)=\varnothing$ if $qd_{1}\geq d_{2}p$ .

#### Proof.

Since the broken lines in consideration do not bend at positive axes, the slopes of their linearity domains can only continue to increase or decrease from the start. Therefore, the order of the terminal slope and the initial slope determines which one of the two sets $\BL_{+}^{0}(p,q)$ and $\BL_{-}^{0}(p,q)$ is empty, unless the broken lines do not bend at all, which is the case $p=q=0$ . ∎

#### Lemma 5.33.

$$ \sum_{t=0}^{p}\pi_{d_{2}-q,t}(p_{1,\bullet})|\BL^{0}_{+}(p-t,q)|=\sum_{t=0}^{q}\pi_{d_{1}-p,t}(p_{2,\bullet})|\BL^{0}_{-}(p,q-t)|. $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma 5.31, it is equivalent to show

$$ \sum_{t=0}^{q}|\BL_{+}^{t}(p,q)|=\sum_{t=0}^{p}|\BL_{-}^{t}(p,q)|. $$

The left-hand side computes the coefficient of $x^{p-d_{1}}y^{q-d_{2}}$ in the theta function $\vartheta_{Q_{+},(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . The right-hand side does the same for $\vartheta_{Q_{-},(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . By Corollary 2.31, they equal. ∎

#### Proposition 5.34.

Fix $(d_{1},d_{2})$ . For any $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , we have

$$ |\BL_{+}^{0}(p,q)|=d_{+}(p,q)\quad\text{and}\quad|\BL_{-}^{0}(p,q)|=d_{-}(p,q). $$

#### Proof.

Compare the recursion of $|\BL_{\pm}^{0}(p,q)|$ determined by Lemma 5.32 and Lemma 5.33 with the recursion of $d_{\pm}(p,q)$ given in Corollary 5.29. ∎

Let $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property Definition 5.9 with $d_{1}\geq ka$ and $d_{2}\geq kb$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 5.17.

We first deal with the case where $d_{1}>ka$ and $d_{2}>kb$ . Suppose that

$$ m=d_{1}b-d_{2}a>0. $$

By the one-bending assumption, every broken line $\beta$ in $\BL_{+}^{0}(ka,kb)$ is of the same bend-type, that is, the only bend is at the ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ with multiplicity $m$ . Notice that $\beta$ indeed reaches the first quadrant. The sum of weight monomials of every $\beta$ in $\BL_{+}^{0}(ka,kb)$ gives the coefficient $\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)$ of $x^{ka}y^{kb}$ in $(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)})^{m}$ . Hence by Proposition 5.34

$$ \lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)=|\BL_{+}^{0}(ka,kb)|=d_{+}(ka,kb). $$

The situation where $m=d_{2}a-d_{1}b>0$ is similar.

Suppose that $d_{1}=ka$ or $d_{2}=kb$ . A one-bending broken line $\beta$ at $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ with initial exponent $(-d_{1},-d_{2})$ and final exponent $(ka-d_{1},kb-d_{2})$ does not reach the first quadrant. So it does not belong to $\BL_{\pm}^{0}(ka,kb)$ . Suppose $d_{2}=kb$ . Then again

$$ m=d_{1}b-d_{2}a>0. $$

Consider the theta function $\vartheta_{Q,(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ for $Q$ chosen generally in the fourth quadrant. By the one-bending property, the sum of the weight of the aforementioned one-bending $\beta$ with endpoint $Q$ is the coefficient $\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)$ . Meanwhile, it also computes the coefficient of $x^{ka-d_{1}}y^{kb-d_{2}}=x^{ka-d_{1}}$ in $\vartheta_{Q,(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . By Corollary 2.31, $\lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)$ equals the coefficient of $x^{ka-d_{1}}$ in $\vartheta_{Q_{+},(-d_{1},-d_{2})}$ . The latter actually equals

$$ |\BL_{+}^{0}(ka,kb)|=d_{+}(ka,kb) $$

because any broken line contributes to $x^{ka-d_{1}}$ must not bend at positive $x$ -axis, thus belonging to $\BL_{+}^{0}(ka,kb)$ . The situation when $d_{1}=ka$ is similar.

Summarizing we have shown

$$ \lambda^{(m)}(ka,kb)=\begin{cases}d_{+}(ka,kb)\quad&\text{if}\ d_{1}b-d_{2}a>0,\\
d_{-}(ka,kb)\quad&\text{if}\ d_{1}b-d_{2}a<0.\end{cases} $$

Finally the polynomials $d_{\pm}(ka,kb)$ are related to weighted counts of shadowed gradings by Lemma 5.23 and Proposition 5.28. ∎

### 5.6. A universal scattering diagram

Recall the monoid $\mathscr{P}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ in Section 2.2. For $\ell_{1}^{\prime}\geq\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}^{\prime}\geq\ell_{2}$ , consider the algebra map

$$ \varphi\colon\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{\ell_{1}^{\prime},\ell_{2}^{\prime}}]}\rightarrow\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}]} $$

that evaluates $p_{1,i}=p_{2,j}=0$ for $i>\ell_{1}$ and $j>\ell_{2}$ .

For any $\ell\geq 1$ , denote

$$ P_{1}^{(\ell)}=1+p_{1,1}x+\dots+p_{1,\ell}x^{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}^{(\ell)}=1+p_{2,1}y+\dots+p_{2,\ell}y^{\ell}. $$

By the functoriality (2.11), we have

$$ \varphi\left(\Scat\left(P_{1}^{(\ell_{1}^{\prime})},P_{2}^{(\ell_{2}^{\prime})}\right)\right)\equiv\Scat\left(P_{1}^{(\ell_{1})},P_{2}^{(\ell_{2})}\right). $$

The scattering diagrams associated to all $(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ thus have a (projective) limit, viewed as a universal scattering diagram. By the tight grading formula Theorem 5.17, the limiting wall-function on $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ is given by

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb}\lambda_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}, $$

where $\lambda_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ is the number of tight gradings of weight polynomial $p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}$ . To recover the wall-function in $\Scat(P_{1}^{(\ell_{1})},P_{2}^{(\ell_{2})})$ , simply let the variables $p_{1,i}$ , $i>\ell_{1}$ and $p_{2,j}$ , $j>\ell_{2}$ be zero. This amounts to considering the subset of tight gradings $\omega$ whose value on horizontal edges is bounded above by $\ell_{2}$ and on vertical edges is bounded above by $\ell_{1}$ .

We note that the limiting structure is more general than the scattering diagrams in Definition 2.3 as the monoid in the limit is not finitely generated. However, one can nonetheless assign degree $k$ to the variable $p_{i,k}$ and have a filtration of ideals $\mathfrak{m}^{(k)}\subseteq\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ generated by elements of degree at least $k$ . Then we can still define scattering diagrams with finitely many walls over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{(k)}$ and a limiting object of those is regarded as a scattering diagram over the completion $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}=\lim\limits_{\longleftarrow}\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{(k)}$ just as in Definition 2.3. Wall-crossing automorphisms and consistency can be discussed analogously.

## 6. Applications of the tight and shadowed grading formulas

Since rank-2 scattering diagrams are known to encode interesting invariants [29, 28, 47, 49], we explore these links in terms of tight and shadowed gradings in this section. We give formulas for computing Euler characteristics of quiver moduli spaces in Section 6.1 and relative Gromov–Witten invariants on toric surfaces in Section 6.2.

### 6.1. Euler characteristics of quiver moduli

We review a result of Reineke and Weist [49] expressing wall-function coefficients in terms of Euler characteristics of certain moduli spaces of quiver representations. Then we establish the link to tight gradings in Corollary 6.3.

In [49] (as well as [29, 28]), the coefficients in the initial wall-functions differ with those in Section 2.2. Precisely, we consider polynomials

$$ P_{1}=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}(1+s_{i}x)\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}(1+t_{j}y) $$

and the scattering diagram $\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ . This setup can be accommodated in the framework of Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 by choosing the monoid $\mathscr{P}=M\oplus\mathbb{M}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{M}_{2}$ where $\mathbb{M}_{1}\cong\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{1}}$ is the (multiplicative) monoid of monomials in $\{s_{1},\dots,s_{\ell_{1}}\}$ and $\mathbb{M}_{2}\cong\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{2}}$ is the monoid of monomials in $\{t_{1},\dots,t_{\ell_{2}}\}$ . The coefficients $p_{1,k}$ and $p_{2,k}$ used in Section 2.2 are elementary symmetric polynomials respectively in $s_{i}$ and in $t_{j}$ by comparing (6.1) with (2.13).

Let $K=K(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})$ be the complete bipartite quiver with $\ell_{1}$ sinks $\{s_{1},\dots,s_{\ell_{1}}\}$ and $\ell_{2}$ sources $\{t_{1},\dots,t_{\ell_{2}}\}$ . For example, $K(3,2)$ is depicted in Figure 6.

*Figure 6. The quiver $K(3,2)$*

Let $\mathbf{P}_{1}=(d_{1,i})_{1\leq i\leq\ell_{1}}$ and $\mathbf{P}_{2}=(d_{2,j})_{1\leq j\leq\ell_{2}}$ be tuples of nonnegative integers. They will be referred to as ordered partitions once we fix the sums $|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=\sum d_{1,i}$ and $|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=\sum d_{2,j}$ . As the notation suggests, $\mathbf{P}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{P}_{2}$ represent two monomials

$$ s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\coloneqq\prod_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}s_{i}^{d_{1,i}}\in\mathbb{M}_{1}\quad\text{and}\quad t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}\coloneqq\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}t_{j}^{d_{2,j}}\in\mathbb{M}_{2}, $$

Meanwhile they also represent a dimension vector $(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ on the quiver $K$ such that the dimension on the sink $s_{i}$ is $d_{1,i}$ and on the source $t_{j}$ is $d_{2,j}$ .

Let $V_{i}=\mathbb{C}^{d_{1,i}}$ for $i=1,\dots,\ell_{1}$ and $W_{j}=\mathbb{C}^{d_{2,j}}$ for $j=1,\dots\ell_{2}$ . Consider the following affine space of representations of $K$ (in $\mathbb{C}$ -vector spaces)

$$ \operatorname{rep}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\coloneqq\{(f_{i,j})_{1\leq i\leq\ell_{1},1\leq j\leq\ell_{2}}\mid f_{i,j}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{C}}(W_{j},V_{i})\}. $$

Let $G=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}\operatorname{GL}(V_{i})\times\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}\operatorname{GL}(W_{j})$ . Then $G$ acts on the two spaces

$$ \operatorname{rep}^{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\coloneqq\operatorname{rep}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\times\prod_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}V_{i}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{rep}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\coloneqq\operatorname{rep}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\times\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}W_{j} $$

respectively by

$$ (g_{i},h_{j})\cdot(f_{i,j},v_{i})=(g_{i}f_{i,j}h_{j}^{-1},g_{i}v_{i})\quad\text{and}\quad(g_{i},h_{j})\cdot(f_{i,j},w_{j})=(g_{i}f_{i,j}h_{j}^{-1},h_{j}w_{j}). $$

The superscripts f and b stand for respectively front and back framing, where the vectors $v_{i}$ and $w_{j}$ are called framing vectors. Elements in $\operatorname{rep}^{\bullet}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ are called framed representations.

We further consider back or front framed representations that are stable in the following sense. We call $(f_{i,j},w_{j})\in\operatorname{rep}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ (resp. $(f_{i,j},v_{i})\in\operatorname{rep}^{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ ) stable if for every tuple $U_{j}\subseteq W_{j}$ of subspaces, we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}\dim f_{i,j}(U_{j})\geq\frac{|\mathbf{P}_{1}|}{|\mathbf{P}_{2}|}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}U_{j}, $$

with strictly inequality if $w_{j}\in U_{j}$ (resp. $v_{i}\in\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}f_{i,j}(U_{j})$ ) for every $j$ (resp. $i$ ). It is clear that framed stable representations are closed under the action of $G$ .

By [49, Corollary 5.4] (based on the construction of [15]), there are smooth irreducible varieties $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})$ as moduli spaces parametrizing respectively back and front framed stable representations up to the action of $G$ . We use $\chi(\cdot)$ to denote the Euler characteristic of a complex variety in analytic topology.

#### Theorem 6.2 ([49, Theorem 6.1]).

For any coprime $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{b} \displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka}\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb}\chi(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}))s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}, \displaystyle\left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{a} \displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka}\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb}\chi(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}))s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}. $$

For coprime $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ and $k\geq 1$ , consider $(d_{1},d_{2})=(kab+1,kb^{2})$ . By Corollary 5.14(2), the vectors $(d_{1},d_{2})$ and $(ka,kb)$ satisfy the one-bending property (Definition 5.9). Notice that $a\cdot kb^{2}-b\cdot(kab+1)=-b$ . Recall from Section 5.3 that by Theorem 5.17, $\lambda^{(b)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ is the number of shadowed gradings on $\mathcal{P}(kab+1,kb^{2})$ of weight monomial $p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}$ where $w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka$ and $w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb$ . Similarly, $\lambda^{(a)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ is the number of shadowed gradings on $\mathcal{P}(ka^{2},kab+1)$ of weight monomial $p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}$ .

We now write down explicit formulas of Euler characteristics of framed stable quiver moduli in terms of counts of shadowed gradings.

#### Corollary 6.3.

For any coprime $(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , ordered partitions $|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka$ , $|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\chi(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})) \displaystyle=\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb}\lambda^{(b)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}, \displaystyle\chi(\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})) \displaystyle=\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb}\lambda^{(a)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}, $$

where $\mu_{\mathbf{P}_{i}}^{\mathbf{Q}_{i}}$ for $i=1,2$ are nonnegative integers defined by the expansions

$$ p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}=\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\quad\text{and}\quad p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}=\sum_{|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

By Theorem 5.17, we can express $\left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}\right)^{b}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka}\sum_{w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb}\lambda^{(b)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}. \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{k\geq 0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka\\
|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb\end{subarray}}\lambda^{(b)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}\right)s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}. $$

Comparing the above coefficients with the ones in Theorem 6.2 we have the desired equation. The other case is similar. ∎

### 6.2. Formula for relative Gromov–Witten invariants

In [29], Gross, Pandharipande, and Siebert expressed the wall-function $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ in terms of relative Gromov–Witten invariants on toric surfaces. We briefly recall their results and give a combinatorial formula for these invariants in Theorem 6.8.

For $(a,b)$ positive and coprime, let $X=X_{a,b}$ denote the toric surface over $\mathbb{C}$ associated to the complete fan generated by rays $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(0,1)$ , $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(1,0)$ , and $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)$ . The three rays correspond to three toric divisors in $X$ which we denote as $D_{1}$ , $D_{2}$ , and $D_{\mathrm{out}}$ .

Fix two positive integers $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ . As in Section 6.1, let $\mathbf{P}_{1}=(d_{1,i})_{1\leq i\leq\ell_{1}}$ and $\mathbf{P}_{2}=(d_{2,j})_{1\leq j\leq\ell_{2}}$ be ordered partitions such that

$$ |\mathbf{P}_{1}|=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}d_{1,i}=ka\quad\text{and}\quad|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}d_{2,j}=kb $$

for some $k\geq 1$ . Consider $\nu\colon X[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]\rightarrow X$ the blow-up of $X$ along $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ general points respectively of $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ away from the $0$ -dimensional toric stratum $S$ (i.e., three toric fixed points). Denote

$$ X^{\circ}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]=X[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]\cut\nu^{-1}(S)\quad\text{and}\quad D_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}=D_{\mathrm{out}}\cut\nu^{-1}(S)\,. $$

Let $\beta\in H_{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})$ be the homology class determined by the intersection numbers

$$ \beta\cdot D_{1}=ak,\quad\beta\cdot D_{2}=bk,\quad\beta\cdot D_{\mathrm{out}}=k. $$

Define the homology class

$$ \beta[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]=\nu^{*}(\beta)-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{1}}d_{1,i}[E_{1,i}]-\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{2}}d_{2,j}[E_{2,j}]\in H_{2}(X[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})],\mathbb{Z}). $$

where $E_{1,i}$ and $E_{2,j}$ are the exceptional divisors over the blown-up points on $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ .

There is a moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ of relative stable maps of genus 0 curves into $X^{\circ}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]$ representing the homology class $\beta[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]$ with full tangency order $k$ at an unspecified point in $D_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}$ . The moduli space $\mathfrak{M}$ is proper of virtual dimension zero and thus the integration over the virtual fundamental class defines a Gromov–Witten type invariant

$$ N_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]\coloneqq\int_{\mathfrak{M}^{\mathrm{vir}}}1\in\mathbb{Q}. $$

We refer the reader to [29, Section 4] for more details on the construction of the moduli space and the definition of $N_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]$ .

#### Theorem 6.5 ([29, Theorem 5.4]).

For any positive coprime $(a,b)$ , we have

$$ \log f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}=\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka\\
|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb\end{subarray}}kN_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}. $$

Combined the above theorem of Gross–Pandharipande–Siebert with the tight grading formula Theorem 5.17, we have the following direct corollary.

#### Corollary 6.7.

We have for any $m\geq 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka\\
|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb\end{subarray}}kN_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb} \displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{m}\log\left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb\end{subarray}}\lambda^{(m)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb}\right)\,. $$

Next we present a formula for each single $N_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]$ that is linear on counts of compatible gradings without involving taking logarithms.

#### Theorem 6.8.

For any $(a,b)$ coprime, $k\geq 1$ and ordered partitions $|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=ka$ and $|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=kb$ , we have

$$ N_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{i}\binom{k}{i}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb\end{subarray}}\lambda^{(i)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})\mu_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}\mu_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Denote $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}=1+Y$ . In the infinite series

$$ \log f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}=Y-\frac{1}{2}Y^{2}+\dots+\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}Y^{k}+\cdots $$

every term with $x^{ka}y^{kb}$ is contained in the part

$$ Y-\frac{1}{2}Y^{2}+\dots+\frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k}Y^{k}=c_{0,k}+c_{1,k}(1+Y)+c_{2,k}(1+Y)^{2}+\dots+c_{k,k}(1+Y)^{k}. $$

By Theorem 5.17, combining the terms with $x^{ka}y^{kb}$ we obtain

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i,k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=ka\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=kb\end{subarray}}\lambda^{(i)}_{a,b}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})p_{1}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}x^{ka}y^{kb} $$

where each $\lambda_{a,b}^{(i)}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})$ counts shadowed gradings. Expand this sum using the expression (6.4) of $p_{i}^{\mathbf{Q}_{i}}$ in terms of $s^{\mathbf{P}_{1}}$ and $t^{\mathbf{P}_{2}}$ and then compare with the right-hand side of (6.6). We see that $N_{(a,b)}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]$ is expressed as desired modulo that $c_{i,k}=\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{i}\binom{k}{i}$ . To compute these numbers, we write each term on the left-hand side of (6.9) as

$$ \frac{(-1)^{j-1}}{j}Y^{j}=\frac{(-1)^{j-1}}{j}(1+Y-1)^{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{j}\binom{j}{i}(1+Y)^{i}. $$

Then we have

$$ c_{i,k}=\sum_{j=i}^{k}\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{j}\binom{j}{i}=\sum_{j=i}^{k}\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{i}\binom{j-1}{i-1}=\frac{(-1)^{i-1}}{i}\binom{k}{i}. $$

∎

In particular, when $k=1$ , we have

$$ N_{a,b}[(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w(\mathbf{Q}_{1})=a\\
w(\mathbf{Q}_{2})=b\end{subarray}}\lambda_{a,b}^{(1)}(\mathbf{Q}_{1},\mathbf{Q}_{2})\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}\mu^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}, $$

where $\lambda_{a,b}^{(1)}$ are honest coefficients of $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(a,b)}$ .

#### Example 6.10.

Let $\ell_{1}=3$ and $\ell_{2}=2$ . Consider the ordered partitions

$$ \mathbf{P}_{1}=3+0+0\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{P}_{2}=3+0. $$

They correspond respectively to the monomials $s_{1}^{3}$ and $t_{1}^{3}$ . Only when $\mathbf{Q}_{1}=p_{1,1}^{3}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{2}=p_{2,1}^{3}$ , we have non-zero coefficients

$$ \mu_{\mathbf{P}_{1}}^{\mathbf{Q}_{1}}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\mu_{\mathbf{P}_{2}}^{\mathbf{Q}_{2}}=1. $$

Then the formula in Theorem 6.8 gives

$$ N_{1,1}[(3+0,3+0+0)]=\frac{1}{3}\left(3\lambda^{(1)}_{1,1}(p_{1,1}^{3},p_{2,1}^{3})-\frac{3}{2}\lambda_{1,1}^{(2)}(p_{1,1}^{3},p_{2,1}^{3})+\frac{1}{3}\lambda^{(3)}_{1,1}(p_{1,1}^{3},p_{2,1}^{3})\right). $$

Using compatible gradings, we can see that only the third term is non-trivial

$$ \lambda^{(3)}_{1,1}(p_{1,1}^{3},p_{2,1}^{3})=1. $$

For this particular grading (depicted in Figure 7), one can choose $(d_{1},d_{2})=(12,9)$ , which with $(ka,kb)=(3,3)$ satisfy the one-bending property by Corollary 5.14. Notice $d_{1}b-d_{2}a=3$ . Therefore, we have computed $N_{1,1}[(3+0,3+0+0)]=1/9$ , which coincides with the multiple cover formula [5] and [29, Proposition 5.2].

## 7. Generalized cluster structures

### 7.1. Generalized cluster structures

Fomin and Zelevinsky’s cluster algebra [18] has been generalized by Chekhov and Shapiro [9] to incorporate polynomial exchange relations (as opposed to binomials). We review the basic notions here.

Let $\mathbb{P}$ be a torsion-free (multiplicative) abelian group, known as the coefficient group [18, 1]. Let $n$ be a positive integer and $I$ denote the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ . We take a field $\mathcal{F}$ isomorphic to the field of rational functions in $n$ independent variables over $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{ZP})$ , the fraction field of $\mathbb{ZP}$ the group ring of $\mathbb{P}$ .

#### Definition 7.1.

A seed in $\mathcal{F}$ is a triple $\Sigma=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},B)$ , where

- • the cluster $\mathbf{x}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}$ is an algebraically independent subset that generates $\mathcal{F}$ over $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{ZP})$ ;

- • the exchange matrix $B=(b_{i,j})$ is a skew-symmetrizable $n\times n$ integer matrix;

- • the coefficient tuples $\mathbf{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{p}_{n})$ consist of, for each $i\in I$ , an $(\ell_{i}+1)$ -tuple $\mathbf{p}_{i}=(p_{i,0},\dots,p_{i,\ell_{i}})$ of elements in $\mathbb{P}$ for $\ell_{i}=\gcd(b_{j,i}\mid j\in I)$ .

For the above data, we refer to any $x_{i}\in\mathbf{x}$ a cluster variable and a monomial in $\mathbf{x}$ a cluster monomial. For $k\in I$ , we define $x_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}$ by the exchange relation

$$ x_{k}x_{k}^{\prime}=P_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{s=0}^{\ell_{k}}p_{k,s}\prod_{b_{i,k}>0}x_{i}^{sb_{i,k}/\ell_{k}}\prod_{b_{j,k}<0}x_{j}^{(s-\ell_{k})b_{j,k}/\ell_{k}}. $$

The set $\mathbf{x}-\{x_{k}\}\cup\{x_{k}^{\prime}\}$ is clearly again an algebraically independent generating set for $\mathcal{F}$ .

#### Definition 7.3.

We say that a seed $\Sigma^{\prime}=(\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{p}^{\prime},B^{\prime})$ in $\mathcal{F}$ is obtained from $\Sigma$ by a seed mutation in direction $k\in I$ if

- • $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\mathbf{x}-\{x_{k}\}\cup\{x_{k}^{\prime}\}$ where $x_{k}^{\prime}$ is defined as in (7.2);

- • the tuples $\mathbf{p}^{\prime}_{i}=(p^{\prime}_{i,0},\dots,p^{\prime}_{i,\ell_{i}})$ satisfy when $i=k$

$$ p^{\prime}_{k,s}=p_{k,\ell_{k}-s},\quad\text{for $s=0,\dots,\ell_{k}$} $$

and when $i\neq k$ , for $s=0,\dots,\ell_{i}$ (7.4)

$$ \frac{p^{\prime}_{i,s}}{p^{\prime}_{i,0}}=\begin{cases}p_{k,\ell_{k}}^{sb_{k,i}/\ell_{i}}\frac{p_{i,s}}{p_{i,0}}\quad&\text{if $b_{k,i}\geq 0$},\\ p_{k,0}^{sb_{k,i}/\ell_{i}}\frac{p_{i,s}}{p_{i,0}}\quad&\text{if $b_{k,i}\leq 0$};\end{cases} $$

- • $B^{\prime}=(b_{i,j}^{\prime})$ is the Fomin–Zelevinsky matrix mutation of $B$ in direction $k$ (denoted as $B^{\prime}=\mu_{k}(B)$ ) given by (7.5)

$$ b_{i,j}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}-b_{i,j}\quad&\text{if $i=k$ or $j=k$},\\ b_{i,j}+[-b_{i,k}]_{+}b_{k,j}+b_{i,k}[b_{k,j}]_{+}\quad&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

It is straightforward to check that a seed mutation is involutive, that is, in the situation of Definition 7.3, the seed $\Sigma$ is also obtained from $\Sigma^{\prime}$ by a seed mutation in direction $k$ . It is worth mentioning that a seed mutation is non-deterministic. For example one sees in (7.4) that uniformly multiplying an element in $\mathbb{P}$ to every $p^{\prime}_{i;s}$ , $s=0,\dots,\ell_{i}$ does not affect the equality.

Let $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ be the $n$ -regular (infinite) tree such that the $n$ edges incident to any vertex are distinctively labeled by $\{1,\dots,n\}$ .

#### Definition 7.6.

A generalized cluster structure in $\mathcal{F}$ is an association of seeds

$$ v\mapsto\Sigma_{v},\quad v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}, $$

such that for any $k$ -labeled edge $v\frac{k}{\hskip 8.19447pt\hskip 8.19447pt}v^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ , the seeds $\Sigma_{v}$ and $\Sigma_{v^{\prime}}$ are obtained from each other by a seed mutation in direction $k$ . When $\ell_{i}=1$ for every $i\in I$ , this is what we refer to as Fomin–Zelevinsky’s ordinary cluster structure [18, 1].

For a seed $\Sigma_{v}=(\mathbf{x}_{v},\mathbf{p}_{v},B_{v})$ associated with $v\in\mathbb{T}_{v}$ , we often use the following notations to denote the gadgets in Definition 7.1:

$$ \mathbf{x}_{v}=\{x_{1;v},\dots,x_{n;v}\},\quad\mathbf{p}_{v}=(\mathbf{p}_{i;v})_{i=1}^{n},\quad\mathbf{p}_{i;v}=(p_{i,s}^{v})_{s=0}^{\ell_{i}},\quad B_{v}=(b^{v}_{i,j}). $$

The first property one would hope a generalized cluster structure to inherit from that of ordinary cluster structures is the Laurent phenomenon [18, Theorem 3.1]. This is indeed the case.

#### Theorem 7.8 ([9, Theorem 2.5]).

In a generalized cluster structure, any cluster variable is expressed in terms of any given cluster as a Laurent polynomial with coefficients in $\mathbb{ZP}$ , that is, for any $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ and any $i\in I$ we have

$$ x_{i;v^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{ZP}[x_{1;v}^{\pm 1},\dots,x_{n;v}^{\pm 1}]. $$

The following is a main result of this paper, the positivity of Laurent phenomenon. Its proof will be given in Section 8.3.

#### Theorem 7.9.

Any cluster variable, when expressed as a Laurent polynomial in any given cluster, has coefficients in $\mathbb{NP}$ , the subset in $\mathbb{ZP}$ of linear combinations in $\mathbb{P}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients.

#### Remark 7.10.

In the case of ordinary cluster structures, the positivity was conjectured originally by Fomin and Zelevinsky in [18], which was first proven by Lee and Schiffler [38] when $B$ is skew-symmetric and then by Gross, Hacking, Keel, and Kontsevich [27] when $B$ is in general skew-symmetrizable. A less general version of Theorem 7.9 was conjectured by Chekhov and Shapiro [9, Section 5] where the coefficient tuples are required to be reciprocal.

### 7.2. Frozen directions and coefficients

In this subsection, every cluster structure is by default generalized. The cluster structure introduced so far can be slightly upgraded by introducing frozen directions of mutations. This amounts to choosing a subset $I_{\mathrm{uf}}\subseteq I$ for unfrozen directions and forbidding mutations in frozen directions $I_{\mathrm{fr}}=I\setminus I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ . By permuting the indices, we can always assume

$$ I_{\mathrm{uf}}=\{1,\dots,|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|\}\subseteq I. $$

So a cluster structure with frozen directions will be defined on the tree $\mathbb{T}_{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}$ . Only the first $|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|$ columns of the exchange matrices will be relevant in exchange relations (7.2) and matrix mutations (7.5).

Since no mutation is performed in frozen directions, all clusters share the same set of frozen cluster variables

$$ \{x_{i}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}\}. $$

Notice that in an exchange polynomial $P_{k}(\mathbf{x})$ we can single out a monomial in frozen variables, combine it with $p_{k,s}$ , and treat them together as a coefficient. The new coefficients

$$ p_{k,s}\prod_{\{i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}\mid b_{i,k}>0\}}x_{i}^{sb_{i,k}/\ell_{k}}\prod_{\{j\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}\mid b_{j,k}<0\}}x_{i}^{(s-\ell_{k})b_{j,k}/\ell_{k}} $$

follow the same mutation rule in Definition 7.3. Hence a cluster structure with frozen directions can be regarded as a special case of Definition 7.6 with the square exchange matrices $(b_{i,j})_{i,j\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}$ . One nuance is to invert frozen variables so that the new coefficients naturally live in the product of $\mathbb{P}$ and the (multiplicative) group of all Laurent monomials in frozen variables.

#### Remark 7.11.

Starting with a cluster structure without frozen directions, we can add frozen directions by extending a square exchange matrix $B$ by adding rows below it, obtaining a rectangular exchange matrix $\widetilde{B}$ . This construction will be useful as later the scattering diagram technique behaves particularly well when $\widetilde{B}$ is of full rank, which can always be achieved by extension.

We now discuss how much that a seed mutation is non-deterministic on coefficients influences cluster variables following Fraser [21, Section 2.4]. For a seed $\Sigma=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},B)$ (with possible frozen directions), define for $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , $s=1,\dots,\ell_{i}$ , monomials

$$ \hat{y}_{i,s}\coloneqq\frac{p_{i,s}}{p_{i,0}}\prod_{j\in I}x_{j}^{sb_{j,i}/\ell_{i}}. $$

#### Proposition 7.13 ([21, Lemma 2.10]).

If for two cluster structures

$$ v\mapsto\Sigma_{v}\quad\text{and}\quad v\mapsto\Sigma_{v}^{\prime},\quad v\in\mathbb{T}_{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}, $$

there is some vertex $v_{0}$ such that $\Sigma_{v_{0}}\sim\Sigma^{\prime}_{v_{0}}$ meaning

$$ \frac{x_{i;v_{0}}}{x_{i;v_{0}}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{P} i\in I \hat{y}_{i,s;v_{0}}=\hat{y}_{i,s;v_{0}}^{\prime} i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}} 1\leq s\leq\ell_{i} $$

then we have $\Sigma_{v}\sim\Sigma_{v}^{\prime}$ for any $v\in\mathbb{T}_{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}$ .

#### Definition 7.14.

Given a (generalized) cluster structure, the associated (generalized) cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is the $\mathbb{ZP}$ -subalgebra of $\mathcal{F}$ generated by all cluster variables

$$ \bigcup_{v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}}\mathbf{x}_{v}=\{x_{i;v}\mid i\in I,v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}\}. $$

The (generalized) upper cluster algebra $\mathcal{U}$ is defined to be the intersection

$$ \bigcap_{v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}}\mathbb{ZP}[x_{i;v}^{\pm 1}\mid i\in I]. $$

It follows from Proposition 7.13 that in any cluster structure where $\Sigma$ is associated to a given vertex $v_{0}$ , any cluster variable in any seed is well-defined up to a factor in $\mathbb{P}$ . Therefore we shall use the notations $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$ and $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}(\Sigma)$ for any seed $\Sigma$ in the cluster structure since $\Sigma$ is sufficient to determine both $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{U}$ . By Theorem 7.8, $\mathcal{A}$ is contained in $\mathcal{U}$ .

#### Remark 7.15.

Another manipulation on a seed $\Sigma$ that does not change $\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$ is to scale the coefficient tuple $\mathbf{p}_{i}=(p_{i,0},\dots,p_{i,\ell_{i}})$ by some uniform factor $p\in\mathbb{P}$ . It follows from Proposition 7.13 that any cluster variable is again well-defined up to a factor in $\mathbb{P}$ . Thus to address the positivity in Theorem 7.9, we can always assume that there is some seed $\Sigma$ where every $p_{i,0}=1$ for $i\in I$ . Moreover, we can take the free abelian group $\mathbb{P}^{\prime}$ generated by symbols

$$ \{p_{i,s}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},1\leq s\leq\ell_{i}\}, $$

with the natural group homomorphism $\psi$ to $\mathbb{P}$ suggested by the notation. Cluster variables generated in the new cluster structure are subtraction-free rational expressions in $|I|$ variables with coefficients in $\mathbb{P}^{\prime}$ . Then $\psi$ induces a map that sends a cluster variable in the new cluster structure to the corresponding cluster variable in the old cluster structure. Therefore once the positivity of Laurent phenomenon is established for $\mathbb{P}^{\prime}$ , it also holds for $\mathbb{P}$ .

## 8. Generalized cluster scattering diagrams

### 8.1. Definitions

We now introduce a construction generalizing Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich’s cluster scattering diagram [27] mostly carried out by Mou [40] and Cheung, Kelley, and Musiker [11]. Here we take a perspective of [3] that both coefficients and frozen directions are present. We impose no reciprocal conditions on coefficients to match the generality in Section 7.1.

The generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ we are about to define is essentially attached to a seed $\Sigma=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},\widetilde{B})$ where $\widetilde{B}$ is a $|I|\times|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|$ rectangular exchange matrix and $p_{i,0}=1$ for any $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ . The coefficient group $\mathbb{P}$ is taken to be the (multiplicative) abelian group freely generated by

$$ \{p_{i,j}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},1\leq j\leq\ell_{i}\}. $$

For easier comparison with [27], we closely follow the language therein (see also [26]) where the information in $\Sigma$ can be easily extracted from the so-called fixed data and seed data.

#### Definition 8.1.

The fixed data $\Gamma$ consists of

- • a lattice $N$ of finite rank with a skew-symmetric bilinear form $\omega\colon N\times N\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}$ ;

- • an unfrozen sublattice $N_{\mathrm{uf}}\subset N$ , a saturated sublattice of $N$ ;

- • an index set $I=\{1,\dots,\operatorname{rank}N\}$ and a subset $I_{\mathrm{uf}}=\{1,\dots,\operatorname{rank}N_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ ;

- • positive integers $d_{i}$ for $i\in I$ with greatest common divisor $1$ ;

- • a sublattice $N^{\circ}\subset N$ of finite index such that $\omega(N_{\mathrm{uf}},N^{\circ})\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ and $\omega(N,N_{\mathrm{uf}}\cap N^{\circ})\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ ;

- • $M=\operatorname{Hom}(N,\mathbb{Z})$ ;

- • a free (multiplicative) abelian group $\mathbb{P}$ of finite rank.

#### Definition 8.2.

Given the fixed data $\Gamma$ , a seed data $\mathbf{s}=(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{p})$ consists of $\mathbf{e}=(e_{i})_{i\in I}\in N^{I}$ and $\mathbf{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{i})_{i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}$ where $\mathbf{p}_{i}=(p_{i,j})_{1\leq j\leq\ell_{i}}$ and $p_{i,j}\in\mathbb{P}$ such that

- (1) $\{e_{i}\mid i\in I\}$ is a basis for $N$ ;

- (2) $\{e_{i}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ is a basis for $N_{\mathrm{uf}}$ ;

- (3) $\{d_{i}e_{i}\mid i\in I\}$ is a basis for $N^{\circ}$ ;

- (4) for $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , the element $w_{i}\coloneqq\omega(-,d_{i}e_{i})/\ell_{i}$ is primitive in $M$ ;

- (5) $\{p_{i,j}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},1\leq j\leq\ell_{i}\}$ is a free generating set for $\mathbb{P}$ .

We impose the following injectivity assumption.

Injectivity assumption: The map

$$ N_{\mathrm{uf}}\cap N^{\circ}\rightarrow M,\quad v\mapsto\omega(-,v) $$

is injective.

Before defining scattering diagrams, we briefly explain how to obtain a seed $\Sigma=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},\widetilde{B})$ from $\Gamma$ and $\mathbf{s}=(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{p})$ . The ambient field $\mathcal{F}$ is the fraction field of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{ZP})[M]$ . Let $\{e_{i}^{*}\in M\mid i\in I\}$ denote the dual basis of $\mathbf{e}$ . The cluster $\mathbf{x}$ in $\Sigma$ is

$$ \{x_{i}\mid i\in I\}=\{x^{e_{i}^{*}}\mid i\in I\}. $$

The coefficient tuples $\mathbf{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{i})_{i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}$ are copied from $\mathbf{s}$ . For $i\in I$ and $j\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , let

$$ b_{i,j}=\omega(e_{i},d_{j}e_{j})\in\mathbb{Z}. $$

Then we put $\widetilde{B}=(b_{i,j})\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|\times|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}$ . The condition that each $\ell_{i}$ divides the $i$ -th column of $\widetilde{B}$ is ensured by (4) of Definition 8.2. The injectivity assumption is then equivalent to that $\widetilde{B}$ is of full rank.

#### Remark 8.4.

It is straightforward to construct fixed and seed data from a seed $\Sigma$ . Let $N=\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}$ and $\{e_{i}\mid i\in I\}$ be the standard basis. For $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , let $d_{i}$ be integers with greatest common divisor $1$ such that the diagonal matrix $(d_{i}\delta_{i,j})_{i,j\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}$ is a left skew-symmetrizer for the first $|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|$ rows of $\widetilde{B}$ . We specify the form $\omega$ , which is determined by $\omega(e_{i},e_{j})$ for $i,j\in I$ . Let

$$ \omega(e_{i},e_{j})=\begin{cases}b_{i,j}/d_{j}\quad&\text{$i\in I$ and $j\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$},\\
-b_{j,i}/d_{i}\quad&\text{$i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ and $j\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}$},\\
0\quad&\text{$i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}$ and $j\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}$}.\end{cases} $$

For any $j\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}=I\setminus I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , set $d_{j}=\operatorname{lcm}(d_{i}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}})$ . With these choices, the conditions in Definition 8.1 and Definition 8.2 are all satisfied.

The scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ will live in the vector space $M_{\mathbb{R}}=M\otimes\mathbb{R}$ . As in the rank- $2$ case, we need a monoid $\mathscr{P}$ with a monoid map $r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M$ . For our purposes in higher ranks, the choice will soon be specified.

Denote by $\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}=\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}_{\mathbf{s}}$ the sub-monoid of $\mathbb{P}$ generated by all $p_{i,s}$ , which is isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{i}}$ (written additively). Let

$$ \mathscr{P}=\mathscr{P}_{\mathbf{s}}\coloneqq M\oplus\mathbb{P}^{\oplus} $$

equipped with the monoid map

$$ r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M,\quad(m,p)\mapsto m. $$

Recall that $\Bbbk$ denotes a ground field of characteristic zero. Analogous to the rank-2 situation, define ideals (the same notation for both)

$$ \mathfrak{m}\coloneqq\mathscr{P}\setminus\mathscr{P}^{\times}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathfrak{m}\coloneqq\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}\setminus\mathscr{P}^{\times}]\subseteq\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}], $$

where $\mathscr{P}^{\times}$ is all units in $\mathscr{P}$ , which is $\{(m,1)\mid m\in M\}$ in the current case. Monomials in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ are associated with elements in $\mathscr{P}$ , thus simply denoted as $px^{m}$ for $(m,p)\in\mathscr{P}$ .

The following definitions of a wall and a scattering diagram are with respect to the fixed data $\Gamma$ and a seed data $\mathbf{s}$ .

#### Definition 8.5.

A wall is the data $\mathfrak{d}$ of

- • the support $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ , a convex rational polyhedral cone of codimension one in $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ with primitive normal vector

$$ n_{\mathfrak{d}}\in N^{+}=N^{+}_{\mathbf{s}}\coloneqq\left\{\sum_{i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}a_{i}e_{i}\,\middle|\,a_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\right\}\setminus\{0\}; $$

- • the wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ , an element in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ of an $\mathfrak{m}$ -primary ideal $I$ or in $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}\coloneqq\lim\limits_{\longleftarrow}\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/{\mathfrak{m}^{k}}$ satisfying

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=1+\sum_{(m,p)\in\mathscr{P}}c_{(m,p)}px^{m}, $$

where $r(m,p)=m\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}})\cap M$ .

For a wall $\mathfrak{d}$ , the primitive generator $m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ of $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}})\cap M$ is called its direction. Any monomial $px^{m}$ that appears in $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ then has $m=km_{\mathfrak{d}}$ for some integer $k\geq 1$ .

#### Definition 8.6.

A scattering diagram over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ for an $\mathfrak{m}$ -primary ideal $I$ is a finite collection of walls whose wall-functions are in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/I$ . A scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ is a countable collection of walls whose wall-functions are in $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ such that for each $k\geq 0$ , the set

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k}\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\mid f_{\mathfrak{d}}\not\equiv 1\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\} $$

is a scattering diagram over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ .

As in the rank-2 situation, we write

$$ \operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}}S_{\mathfrak{d}}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}}\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}\cup\bigcup_{\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}(S_{\mathfrak{d}}\cap S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}) $$

for the support and singular locus of $\mathfrak{D}$ where the last union is taken over all pairs of walls such that the intersection of their supports is of dimension $\dim M_{\mathbb{R}}-2$ .

Wall-crossing automorphisms are defined by the higher-rank analogue of (2.5), which act on the complete algebra $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ . The notion of a path-ordered product $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma,\mathfrak{D}}$ is also extended verbatim to the higher-rank situation for a regular path $\gamma$ that avoids $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ and whose endpoints avoid $\operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})$ . The equivalence relation between scattering diagrams and the consistency of a scattering diagram are defined in the same way as respectively in Definition 2.6 and Definition 2.8.

#### Definition 8.8.

A wall $\mathfrak{d}$ is said to be incoming if its direction $m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ (or equivalently $\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}})$ ) is contained in the support $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . Otherwise it is called non-incoming or outgoing.

Consider the initial scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}}\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{d}_{i}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}\quad\text{where}\quad S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}\coloneqq e_{i}^{\perp}\quad\text{and}\quad f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}\coloneqq 1+\sum_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,1}x^{jw_{i}}. $$

Clearly every wall in $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}}$ is incoming.

The following result slightly generalizes [27, Theorem 1.12] and is again a consequence of [34, 2.1.6]; see [40, Section 6.2] and [11, Section 3.2].

#### Theorem 8.9.

There is a scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ satisfying:

- (1) $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is consistent,

- (2) $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}\subseteq\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}}$ ,

- (3) $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}\setminus\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}}$ consists only of outgoing walls.

Moreover, $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is unique up to equivalence.

When $p_{i,0}$ and $p_{i,\ell_{i}}$ specialize to $1$ and any $p_{i,j}$ , $j\notin\{0,\ell_{i}\}$ specializes to $0$ (then $f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}$ becoming a binomial) for any $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , then $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is what now known as the cluster scattering diagram of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich [27, Section 1.1]. We call $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ defined by Theorem 8.9 a generalized cluster scattering diagram.

#### Remark 8.10.

When $I_{\mathrm{uf}}=I$ and $|I|=2$ , then $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ can be easily transformed to the generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ considered in Section 2.2 by a piecewise linear transformation as in Theorem 2.16.

Our main novel result concerning $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ is the positivity of its wall-functions, Theorem 8.11, from which all remaining positivity results follow. The proof will be given in Section 9.

#### Theorem 8.11.

There is a representative (in the equivalence class) of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ such that for any wall $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ , the wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ belongs to $\widehat{\mathbb{N}[\mathscr{P}]}$ , that is,

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=1+\sum_{(m,p)\in\mathscr{P}}c_{(m,p)}px^{m} $$

has nonnegative integer coefficients $c_{(m,p)}$ .

### 8.2. The cluster complex structure

The scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ possesses a cluster complex structure as in the rank-2 situation. This structure is important for uncovering the connection with the corresponding generalized cluster algebra and is thus essential to the proof of Theorem 7.9. In the ordinary case, the cluster complex structure is described in [27]. In the generalized case, the underlying cone complex is exactly the same [40, 11], which only depends on the exchange matrix $\widetilde{B}$ . The more involved part in this generalization is the description of wall-functions (Theorem 8.20) due to the complication of coefficients.

We need some preparations. Let $B$ be a skew-symmetrizable $n\times n$ matrix associated to a chosen root $v_{0}\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ . Then for each $v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ , we define inductively $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors

$$ \mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}=\left(c_{j;v}^{(i)}\,\middle|\,j=1,\dots,n\right)\in\mathbb{N}^{n}\ \text{or}\ \mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{n},\quad\text{for}\quad i=1,\dots,n $$

by the following rule. Set initially

$$ \mathbf{c}_{v_{0}}^{(i)}\coloneqq(\delta_{i,j}\mid j=1,\dots,n),\quad i=1,\dots,n, $$

the standard unit vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ . For an edge $v\frac{k}{\hskip 8.19447pt\hskip 8.19447pt}v^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ , their associated $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors satisfy

$$ \mathbf{c}_{v^{\prime}}^{(i)}=\begin{cases}-\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(k)}\quad&\text{if $i=k$;}\\
\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}+b_{k,i}^{v}[\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(k)}]_{+}\quad&\text{if $i\neq k$ and $b_{i,k}^{v}\leq 0$;}\\
\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}+b_{k,i}^{v}[-\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(k)}]_{+}\quad&\text{if $i\neq k$ and $b_{i,k}^{v}>0$}.\end{cases} $$

Notice that the relation (8.12) is reflexive for $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ . Therefore, we have well-defined $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}$ for any $v$ by propagating (8.12) along $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ starting from $v_{0}$ . The $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors were developed by Fomin and Zelevinsky in [20] as a useful tool to study the dynamics of coefficients.

#### Theorem 8.13 ([27, Corollary 5.5]).

The $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors are always sign coherent, that is, each $\mathbf{c}$ -vector $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}$ for $i=1,\dots,n$ and $v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ is either in $\mathbb{N}^{n}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{n}$ .

#### Remark 8.14.

The sign coherence of $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors was conjectured in [20, Conjecture 5.4 and Proposition 5.6(iii)]. In the skew-symmetric case, it was proven by Derksen, Weyman and Zelevinsky [14] using quiver representations. More generally, for any skew-symmetrizable exchange matrix, the sign coherence was proven in [27] using scattering diagram techniques. It also follows that the vectors $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(n)}$ form a basis in $\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ ; see the proof of [20, Proposition 5.6].

It is straightforward from the recurrence (8.12) that

$$ c_{i;v}^{(i)}+1\quad\text{or}\quad c_{i;v}^{(i)}-1 $$

is divisible by $\ell_{i}$ , and $c_{j;v}^{(i)}$ is divisible by $\ell_{i}$ when $j\neq i$ .

#### Definition 8.15.

Define non-negative integers

$$ h_{j;v}^{(i)}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\frac{|c_{i;v}^{(i)}\pm 1|}{\ell_{i}}\in\mathbb{N}\quad&\text{if $i=j$};\\
\frac{|c_{j;v}^{(i)}|}{\ell_{i}}\in\mathbb{N}\quad&\text{if $i\neq j$}.\end{cases} $$

#### Remark 8.17.

When $\ell_{i}=1$ or $2$ , there is ambiguity on $h_{i;v}^{(i)}$ . However, it does not affect the description in Theorem 8.20.

For given seed data $\mathbf{s}$ with $\mathbf{e}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}$ and $B=(b_{i,j})=\omega(e_{i},d_{j}e_{j})$ for $i,j\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ . we define another set of vectors $g^{*}_{i;v}\in N_{\mathrm{uf}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ again indexed by $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ . These are called dual $g$ -vectors. The relation they need to satisfy is analogous to (8.12) but with respect to $-B^{\intercal}$ . Explicitly we set initially

$$ g^{*}_{i;v_{0}}\coloneqq e_{i},\quad i=1,\dots,n, $$

and for $v\frac{k}{\hskip 8.19447pt\hskip 8.19447pt}v^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{T}_{n}$ , put the relation

$$ g_{i;v^{\prime}}^{*}=\begin{cases}-g_{k;v}^{*}\quad&\text{if $i=k$;}\\
g_{i;v}^{*}-b_{i,k}^{v}[g_{k;v}^{*}]_{+}\quad&\text{if $i\neq k$ and $b_{i,k}^{v}\leq 0$;}\\
g_{i;v}^{*}-b_{i,k}^{v}[-g_{k;v}^{*}]_{+}\quad&\text{if $i\neq k$ and $b_{i,k}^{v}>0$}.\end{cases} $$

For the same reason as $\mathbf{c}$ -vectors, they are sign-coherent by Theorem 8.13 and $(g_{1;v}^{*},\dots,g_{n;v}^{*})$ form a basis of $N_{\mathrm{uf}}$ . Moreover, $g_{i;v}^{*}$ (in the basis $\mathbf{e}$ ) and $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}_{v}$ always have the same sign (see [44, (2,7)]), which we denote by

$$ \varepsilon_{i;v}\coloneqq\begin{cases}1\quad&\text{if $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}_{v}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}$},\\
-1\quad&\text{if $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}_{v}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{n}$}.\end{cases} $$

Define for each $v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ , the convex cone

$$ \mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}\coloneqq\{m\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\mid\langle m,g_{i;v}^{*}\rangle\geq 0,\ i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}\subseteq M_{\mathbb{R}}. $$

It has $n$ facets

$$ S_{i;v}\coloneqq(g_{i;v}^{*})^{\perp}\cap\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+},\quad i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}. $$

One can verify inductively that

$$ w_{i;v}\coloneqq\omega(-,\frac{d_{i}}{\ell_{i}}\varepsilon_{i;v}g_{i;v}^{*})\in M. $$

Now we are ready to state the cluster complex structure of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ .

#### Theorem 8.20.

There is a pure $|I|$ -dimensional cone complex $\Delta^{+}_{\mathbf{s}}$ in $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ whose top-dimensional cones are

$$ \{\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}\mid v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}\}. $$

In its equivalent class, $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ has a representative containing the collection of walls

$$ \mathfrak{D}(\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+})\coloneqq\{(S_{i;v},f_{i;v})\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}\} $$

where

$$ f_{i;v}=\begin{cases}1+\sum_{s=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,s}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{sh_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{sw_{i;v}}\quad&\text{if $\ell_{i}h_{i;v}^{(i)}=|c_{i;v}^{(i)}|-1$}\\
1+\sum_{s=1}^{\ell_{i}}\frac{p_{i,\ell_{i}-s}}{p_{i,\ell_{i}}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{sh_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{sw_{i;v}}\quad&\text{if $\ell_{i}h_{i;v}^{(i)}=|c_{i;v}^{(i)}|+1$}\end{cases} $$

such that $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}\setminus\mathfrak{D}(\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+})$ has support disjoint from (the codimension $\leq 1$ strata of) $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ .

#### Proof.

The cone complex $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ is understood and has equivalent description in [27, Section 4 and 5]. We thus focus on deriving the claimed expression of wall-functions from [40, Theorem 7.10]. There $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ has initial wall-functions for $i=1,\dots,n$

$$ \prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}(1+t_{i,j}x^{w_{i}}) $$

where $t_{i,j}$ are formal variables. While these were denoted as $p_{i,j}$ in [40], we change everything there from the letter $p$ to $t$ in order to avoid conflict with our coefficients $p_{i,s}$ . In fact, we can regard $p_{i,s}$ as symmetric polynomials of $t_{i,j}$ by equating

$$ 1+\sum_{s=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,s}x^{sw_{i}}=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}(1+t_{i,j}x^{w_{i}}). $$

In particular we have $p_{i,\ell_{i}}=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}t_{i,j}$ .

The wall-function $f_{i;v}$ is expressed in [40, Theorem 7.10] as

$$ f_{i;v}=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell_{i}}\left(1+t_{i,j;v}^{\varepsilon_{i;v}}x^{w_{i;v}}\right)\quad\text{where}\quad\varepsilon_{i;v}=\begin{cases}1\quad&\text{if $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}_{v}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}$},\\
-1\quad&\text{if $\mathbf{c}^{(i)}_{v}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{n}$},\end{cases} $$

and each $t_{i,j;v}$ is a monomial in $\{t_{i,j}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},j=1,\dots,\ell_{i}\}$ . The exponent vector of $t_{i,j;v}$ is termed as a generalized $c$ -vector and has the same sign $\varepsilon_{i;v}$ as $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}$ ([40, Proposition 3.17]). By [40, Lemma 3.15 and Lemma 3.16], the monomial $t_{i,j;v}$ (simultaneously for all $j=1,\dots,\ell_{i}$ ) is of the form

$$ t_{i,j}\cdot p_{i,\ell_{i}}^{\frac{c_{i;v}^{(i)}-1}{\ell_{i}}}\cdot\prod_{j\neq i}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{\frac{c_{j;v}^{(i)}}{\ell_{j}}}\quad\text{or}\quad t_{i,j}^{-1}\cdot p_{i,\ell_{i}}^{\frac{c_{i;v}^{(i)}+1}{\ell_{i}}}\cdot\prod_{j\neq i}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{\frac{c_{j;v}^{(i)}}{\ell_{j}}}\,. $$

We assume the former case and the latter one can be similarly treated. Now there are two further cases.

Case 1: $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}$ . This means

$$ \ell_{i}h_{i;v}^{(i)}=c_{i;v}^{(i)}-1\quad\text{and}\quad\ell_{j}h_{j;v}^{(i)}=c_{i;v}^{(i)}. $$

Then we can express $f_{i;v}$ as

$$ \prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{i}}\left(1+t_{i,k}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{h_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{w_{i;v}}\right)=1+\sum_{s=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,s}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{sh_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{sw_{i;v}}, $$

proving the first scenario of (8.21).

Case 2: $\mathbf{c}_{v}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}^{n}$ . In this case, we have

$$ \ell_{i}h_{i;v}^{(i)}=-c_{i;v}^{(i)}+1\quad\text{and}\quad\ell_{j}h_{j;v}^{(i)}=-c_{i;v}^{(i)}. $$

We can then express $f_{i;v}$ as

$$ \prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{i}}\left(1+t_{i,k}^{-1}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{h_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{w_{i;v}}\right)=1+\sum_{s=1}^{\ell_{i}}\frac{p_{i,\ell_{i}-s}}{p_{i,\ell_{i}}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}p_{j,\ell_{j}}^{sh_{j;v}^{(i)}}x^{sw_{i;v}}. $$

This verifies the second scenario of (8.21). ∎

### 8.3. Theta functions and positivity of the Laurent phenomenon

Broken lines can also be defined in higher ranks. It suffices for our purposes to consider the initial exponent in $M$ . We treat $\Bbbk[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ as the coefficient ring and thus express a monomial (with coefficient) in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]$ as $cx^{m}$ where $c\in\Bbbk[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ and $m\in M$ .

#### Definition 8.23.

Let $m_{0}\in M\setminus\{0\}$ and $Q\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\cut\Supp(\mathfrak{D})$ . A broken line $\beta$ for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ is a piecewise linear continuous proper path

$$ \beta\colon(-\infty,0]\to M_{\mathbb{R}}\cut\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}) $$

with values $-\infty=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{\ell+1}=0$ and an associated monomial $c_{i}x^{m_{i}}\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ for each interval $(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})$ , $i=0,\dots,\ell$ such that

- (1) $\beta(0)=Q$ and $c_{0}=1$ ;

- (2) $\dot{\beta}(\tau)=-m_{i}$ for any $\tau\in(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})$ for each $i=0,\dots,\ell$ ;

- (3) the subpath $\beta|_{(\tau_{i-1},\tau_{i+1})}$ transversally crosses the support of some wall at $\tau_{i}$ for $i=1,\dots,\ell-1$ ;

- (4) for $i=0,\dots,\ell-1$ , $c_{i+1}x^{m_{i+1}}$ is a monomial term (other than $c_{i}x^{m_{i}}$ ) of the power series

$$ c_{i}x^{m_{i}}\prod_{\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\mid\beta(\tau_{i})\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{n_{i}\cdot m_{i}} $$

where $n_{i}$ is primitive in $N$ and orthogonal to any $\mathfrak{d}$ with $\beta(\tau_{i})\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ such that $n_{i}\cdot r(m_{i})>0$ .

As in rank $2$ , a theta function is defined to be the formal sum of the final monomial terms of broken lines. Precisely, the theta function associated to $m_{0}$ and $Q$ is

$$ \vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}\coloneqq\sum_{\beta}c(\beta)x^{m(\beta)}, $$

the sum of all final monomials over all broken line for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ .

We summarize in below the main properties of theta functions that we will need.

#### Proposition 8.25.

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a scattering diagram. Let $m_{0}\in M\setminus\{0\}$ and $Q\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D})$ .

- (1) The theta function $\vartheta_{Q,m_{0}}$ lives in $x^{m_{0}}\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ .

- (2) Let $\mathfrak{D}=\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ , and let $Q\in\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+})$ and $m\in\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}\cap M$ . Then $\vartheta_{Q,m}=x^{m}$ .

#### Proof.

(1) generalizes [27, Proposition 3.4]. The settings slightly differ as our monoid $\mathscr{P}$ contains the coefficient part $\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}$ . The proof nonetheless does not change.

(2) generalizes [27, Corollary 3.9]. It follows from generalizing [27, Proposition 3.8] and [27, Proposition 3.6] to our setting. The former is the special case when $v=v_{0}$ and carries over by the same argument. The latter is a bijection between certain broken lines in $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ and $\mathfrak{D}_{\mu_{k}(\mathbf{s})}$ . We have not defined the mutation $\mu_{k}(\mathbf{s})$ but it can be understood as in [40, Definition 6.3] by unveiling the relation between the variables $t_{i,j}$ and $p_{i,s}$ (8.22). Then we can refer to [40, Proposition 8.9]. ∎

Let $\Sigma$ be a seed arising from $\Gamma$ and $\mathbf{s}=(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{p})$ as in Section 8.1. Consider the generalized cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)$ .

#### Theorem 8.26.

There is a generalized cluster structure such that $\Sigma_{v_{0}}=\Sigma$ and the cluster monomials in $\mathcal{A}$ (with frozen variables inverted)

$$ \left\{\prod_{i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}}x_{i;v}^{a_{i}}\prod_{j\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}}x_{j;v}^{b_{j}}\,\middle|\,a_{i}\in\mathbb{N},b_{j}\in\mathbb{Z},v\in\mathbb{T}_{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}\right\} $$

are precisely the theta functions

$$ \{\vartheta_{Q,m}\mid m\in\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}\cap M\} $$

for a general $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{v_{0}}^{+}$ .

#### Proof.

In the ordinary case, this is [27, Theorem 4.9]. The generalized case is discussed in [40, Section 8.4] (and also in [11] with reciprocal coefficients) and essentially relies on Theorem 8.20 the cluster complex structure of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ . We elaborate more as the setup here differs slightly.

In [40], we assume $I_{\mathrm{uf}}=I$ namely without any frozen directions. Hence in that case the maximal cones in $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ are all simplicial whose (primitive) generators are called $g$ -vectors. With frozen directions, we can still define $g$ -vectors (using the same recurrence)

$$ \{g_{i;v}\in M\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}. $$

The difference caused by frozen directions is that the recurrence to define $g$ -vectors only uses the rectangular exchange matrix $\widetilde{B}$ (and its mutations). Another option is to extend $I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ to $I$ per the construction in Remark 8.4. Now we have a $|I|\times|I|$ square exchange matrix which can be used to define the dual $g$ -vectors $\{g_{i;v}^{*}\in N\mid i\in I\}$ for any $v\in\mathbb{T}_{|I|}$ . Then $\{g_{i;v}\in M\mid i\in I\}$ can be defined to be the dual basis in $M$ and we only take the ones with $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ .

The vectors $\{g_{i;v}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ are dual to $\{g_{i;v}^{*}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ in the sense that $\langle g_{i;v},g_{j;v}^{*}\rangle=\delta_{i,j}$ . The cone $\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}$ has the description

$$ \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}}\{g_{i;v}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}\oplus\bigoplus_{i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}}\mathbb{R}e_{i}^{*}. $$

Any $m\in\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}\cap M$ is a sum of a nonnegative integral sum of $\{g_{i;v}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ and a vector $m_{\mathrm{fr}}\in\bigoplus_{i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}}\mathbb{Z}e_{i}^{*}$ . In [40], the mutation of a seed is deterministic so we can generate a cluster structure from $\Sigma_{v_{0}}=\Sigma$ , which can be extracted from Theorem 8.20. In particular, by [40, Proposition 8.1], the unfrozen cluster variable $x_{i;v}$ is given by

$$ x_{i;v}=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(x^{g_{i;v}})\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]} $$

for a regular path $\gamma$ going from $\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}$ to $\mathcal{C}_{v_{0}}^{+}$ .
