Any wall-crossing automorphism acts trivially on $x^{m_{\mathrm{fr}}}$ , which is a Laurent monomial of frozen variables $\{x^{e_{i}^{*}}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{fr}}\}$ . Now we see that any cluster monomial (with frozen variables inverted) equals

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(x^{m})\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]} $$

for $m$ in $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}\cap M$ .

To see that any $\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(x^{m})$ for $m\in\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}\cap M$ is a theta function, we first have by Proposition 8.25

$$ \vartheta_{Q_{v},m}=x^{m} $$

for any $m\in\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}\cap M$ and any $Q_{v}$ in the interior of $\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}$ . Then using a higher-rank analogue of Theorem 2.29 (see [27, Theorem 3.5] and [8]), we have

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(x^{m})=\mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(\vartheta_{Q_{v},m})=\vartheta_{Q,m}. $$

for a general $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{v_{0}}^{+}$ . ∎

Now we show the positivity of Laurent phenomenon for cluster monomials in any generalized cluster structure (with possible frozen directions). See the statement in Theorem 7.9 and terminologies in Section 7.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 7.9.

If suffices to show this when the (rectangular) exchange matrix $B$ has full rank. If not, we can add more frozen directions by adding rows to $B$ to get a full rank matrix. Evaluating added frozen variables at $1$ recovers original cluster monomials.

Another simplification is to assume $p_{i,0}=1$ for any $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ as discussed in Remark 7.15. Now with the injectivity assumption (8.3) ensured by the full rank of $B$ , the generalized cluster structure is contained within the scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ where $\mathbf{s}$ can be constructed from a seed $\Sigma=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},B)$ as in Remark 8.4.

Now every cluster monomial is a theta function $\vartheta_{Q,m}$ by Theorem 8.26. Now the positivity of the Laurent phenomenon follows from Theorem 7.8 and that the weight $c(\gamma)$ of every broken line $\gamma$ is in $\mathbb{N}\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}$ due to the positivity of wall-functions Theorem 8.11. ∎

There are variants of Chekhov–Shapiro’s generalized cluster structures, for example [43, 22, 40], where certain restrictions are imposed on coefficients so that coefficients are “normalized” and thus mutations are deterministic. These settings can nonetheless be viewed as special cases of Definition 7.6 as pointed out in loc. cit. Therefore, the positivity Theorem 7.9 is still valid in those settings.

### 8.4. Strong positivity of theta functions

We define structure constants for theta functions following [27, Definition-Lemma 6.2], with the difference that now they are not just integers but in the coefficient ring $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ . The argument carries over and the positivity follows directly from Theorem 8.11. Remind that we are given a generalized cluster scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ .

#### Definition-Lemma 8.29.

Let $p_{1},p_{2},q\in M$ . Let $z\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ be chosen generally. There are at most finitely many pairs of broken lines $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}$ with $m_{0}(\gamma_{1})=p_{1}$ , $m_{0}(\gamma_{2})=p_{2}$ and both ending at $z$ , and $m(\gamma_{1})+m(\gamma_{2})=q$ . Define

$$ \alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};q)=\sum_{(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2})}c(\gamma_{1})c(\gamma_{2}) $$

where the finite sum is over the aforementioned pairs of broken lines. Hence $\alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ is in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ by Theorem 8.11.

Now we can describe the product structure of theta functions using $\alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ . Let $Q$ be general in $\mathcal{C}_{v_{0}}^{+}$ . Write $\vartheta_{m}=\vartheta_{m,Q}$ for any $m\in M$ . The fact that the structure constants $\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ are in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ is what we refer to as the strong positivity.

#### Theorem 8.30 (cf. [27, Proposition 6.4(3)]).

The theta functions $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ form a topological basis of certain formal completion of a variant $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}$ of the upper cluster algebra $\mathcal{U}$ . For any $p_{1},p_{2}\in M$ , we have

$$ \vartheta_{p_{1}}\cdot\vartheta_{p_{2}}=\sum_{q\in M}\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};q)\vartheta_{q}\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]} $$

where $\alpha(p_{1},p_{2},q)\coloneqq\alpha_{z(q)}(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ for $z(q)$ chosen sufficiently near $q$ and is independent of this choice.

#### Proof.

The proof essentially follows that of [27, Proposition 6.4(3)]. We first understand conceptually where the theta functions live. In fact, for each $v\in\mathbb{T}_{v}$ , we have the algebra

$$ \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}][x_{i;v}^{\pm 1}\mid i\in I]\subseteq\mathcal{F}. $$

Denote the intersection of all these algebras by $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}$ (by $\mathcal{U}$ if taking the coefficient ring $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ instead). It contains all cluster monomials. In fact, when expressing $x_{i;v}$ in another cluster $\mathbf{x}_{v^{\prime}}$ , it is the theta function $\vartheta_{Q_{v^{\prime}},g_{i;v}}$ for some general $Q_{v^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{C}_{v^{\prime}}^{+}$ by (8.27) and (8.28), so the coefficients are actually in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ . Take the completion

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}\coloneqq\lim_{\longleftarrow}\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}/I^{k} $$

with respect to the ideal $I$ generated by $\{p_{i,s}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}},1\leq s\leq\ell_{i}\}$ . For the same reason $\mathcal{U}$ contains cluster monomials, $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ contains the theta functions $\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in M\}$ .

We note that $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}/I=\Bbbk[M]$ since letting $p_{i,s}=0$ makes any $\vartheta_{Q_{v^{\prime}},g_{i;v}}$ a single monomial $x^{g_{i;v}}$ . This phenomenon is phrased in [27, Corollary 5.3] as the central fiber of the family $\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{prin}}^{\mathbf{s}}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}}^{n}$ is the torus $T_{N}$ . Here we are directly taking the regular functions instead of considering the relevant schemes. The family is in the ordinary case, thus recovered by restricting to all $p_{i,s}=0$ except for the leading ones $\{p_{i,\ell_{i}}\mid i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}\}$ , which correspond to the coordinates $\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}$ .

Back to the product structure, now it suffices to show (8.31) in $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}/I^{k+1}$ for each $k\geq 0$ . Now the theta functions can be defined using the finite scattering diagram $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ . As argued in the first paragraph of the proof of [27, Proposition 6.4], theta functions $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ form a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]/I^{k+1}$ -basis for $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}/I^{k+1}$ ; it is clear when $k=0$ as $\vartheta_{q}=x^{q}$ and one can use Nakayama’s lemma to lift the basis $\{x^{q}\mid q\in M\}$ to $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ in $\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}/I^{k+1}$ . We thus say that $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ form a topological basis of $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ .

For a given $k\geq 1$ , express $\vartheta_{p_{1}}\cdot\vartheta_{p_{2}}$ in the basis $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ . Notice we can choose any general terminal point for this expression because for different terminal points, theta functions are transformed under a path-ordered product which does not change coefficients in $\Bbbk[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]/I^{k}$ . For a given $q\in M$ , choose a general terminal point $z$ close enough to $q$ so that they belong to the same chamber. By the definition of $\alpha_{z}$ , we have

$$ \vartheta_{z,p_{1}}\cdot\vartheta_{z,p_{2}}=\sum_{r}\alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};r)x^{r}. $$

However, among all broken lines for all $\vartheta_{z,r}$ , $r\in M$ , there is only one broken line (whose image is $z+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}q$ ) with associated final monomial $x^{q}$ , which gives the theta function $\vartheta_{z,q}=x^{q}$ . Thus the coefficient of $\vartheta_{z,q}$ can be read off by the coefficient of $x^{q}$ on the right-hand side of (8.32), namely $\alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ . This proves the product formula in order $k$ . To see the independence of $z$ for all $k$ , we observe exactly as in the proof of [27, Definition-Lemma 6.2] that for given $p_{1},p_{2},q$ only finitely many wall-function terms in $\mathfrak{D}$ are relevant to the possible pairs of broken lines computing $\alpha_{z}(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ (for any general $z$ ). Hence one can choose a big enough $k$ and use $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ to define $\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};q)$ . ∎

In general, the cluster complex $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ is only a proper subset of $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ . Theta functions outside $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ may not be Laurent but a formal sum. The following observation generalizes [27, Proposition 7.1] immediately once we have the positivity of wall-crossing functions Theorem 8.11.

#### Proposition 8.33.

Let $m_{0}\in M$ . If for some general point $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{v}^{+}$ for $v\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ there are only finitely many broken lines for $m_{0}$ with endpoint $Q$ , the same is true for any general point $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{v^{\prime}}^{+}$ for any other $v^{\prime}\in\mathbb{T}_{n}$ . In this case, the theta function $\vartheta_{m}$ is a positive universal Laurent polynomial.

We can now extend [27, Theorem 7.5] to the generalized case.

#### Theorem 8.34.

Let $\Theta\subseteq M$ be the collection of $m$ such that the theta function $\vartheta_{m}$ is a finite sum, that is, by Proposition 8.33 a universal Laurent polynomial.

- (1) $\Delta_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}\cap M\subseteq\Theta$ .

- (2) For $p_{1},p_{2}\in\Theta$ ,

$$ \vartheta_{p_{1}}\cdot\vartheta_{p_{2}}=\sum_{r}\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};r)\vartheta_{r} $$

is a finite sum with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ . If $\alpha(p_{1},p_{2};r)\neq 0$ , then $r\in\Theta$ .

- (3) $\Theta$ is a saturated monoid in $M$ .

- (4) The $\Bbbk[\mathbb{P}]$ -module

$$ \mathcal{M}\coloneqq\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]}\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in\Theta\} $$

is an associative $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -algebra with a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -basis given by $\{\vartheta_{m}\mid m\in\Theta\}$ . We have natural inclusions

$$ \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{U}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof uses the exact same arguments as in [27, Theorem 7.5] but relies on the generalized positivity Theorem 8.11. We note that the inclusion $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{M}$ sends a cluster monomial to the corresponding theta function given by Theorem 8.26 and the second inclusion $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{U}$ is guaranteed by Proposition 8.33. ∎

#### Remark 8.35.

In the ordinary case, the algebra $\mathcal{M}$ is denoted as $\operatorname{mid}(\mathcal{A})$ (where $\mathcal{A}$ denotes the cluster variety) and called the middle cluster algebra in [27]. The set $\Theta$ a priori depends on the choices of $\ell_{i}$ . In particular, when $\ell_{i}=1$ for any $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ , it is the corresponding set for ordinary cluster algebras. It is interesting to ask whether the generalized and ordinary situations share the same $\Theta$ .

### 8.5. Theta functions are atomic

A non-zero element in the upper cluster algebra $\mathcal{U}$ is called universally positive [17] if it is a Laurent polynomial with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}]$ in every cluster, that is, it is in the subset

$$ \bigcap_{v\in\mathbb{T}_{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}}\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}][x_{i;v}^{\pm 1}\mid i\in I]\subseteq\mathcal{U}. $$

Such an element is furthermore called indecomposable or atomic if it cannot be written as a sum of two universally positive elements. Any cluster monomial is universally positive by Theorem 7.9 and is atomic since it is a monomial in some cluster.

Theta functions are not necessarily in $\mathcal{U}$ but live in the completion $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ . We follow Mandel’s definition [39] of atomicity using the scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ .

#### Definition 8.36.

A non-zero element $f\in\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ is called universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas if regarded as an element in $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ , for any general $Q\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{s}}^{+}$ , any general $Q^{\prime}\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})$ , and a regular path $\gamma$ from $Q$ to $Q^{\prime}$ , the element

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(f)\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]} $$

is a formal Laurent series with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ . It is in addition called atomic if it cannot be written as a sum of two elements that are universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas.

#### Theorem 8.37 (cf. [39, Theorem 1]).

The theta functions $\{\vartheta_{q}\mid q\in M\}$ (up to a scalar in $\mathbb{P}$ ) are exactly the atomic elements of $\widehat{\mathcal{U}^{\oplus}}$ with respect to the scattering atlas.

#### Proof.

It follows directly from Theorem 8.11 and ([27, Theorem 3.5] and [8])

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(\vartheta_{Q,q})=\vartheta_{Q^{\prime},q} $$

that theta functions are universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas. Then it remains to show that for any $f$ universally positive with respect to the scattering atlas, the expansion

$$ f=\sum_{q\in M}a_{q}\vartheta_{q} $$

has $a_{q}\in\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ for any $q\in M$ . However, for $r\in M$ , we can take $Q^{\prime}$ sufficiently close to $r$ as in the proof of Theorem 8.30 so that in the expansion

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{\gamma}(f)=\sum_{q\in M}c_{q}x^{q}, $$

we have $a_{r}=c_{r}\in\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}]$ by the universal positive assumption on $f$ . ∎

## 9. Positivity of wall-functions

This section is devoted to positivity of scattering diagrams. We prove in Section 9.2 that in rank 2, any consistent scattering diagram is positive with respect to the initial coefficients. In Section 9.3, we prove Theorem 8.11, the positivity of higher-rank generalized cluster scattering diagrams.

### 9.1. The non-standard case

The scattering diagrams considered in Section 2.2 are regarded as standard, as the directions of the two initial walls are standard unit vectors $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ . The non-standard case can be treated by the change-of-lattice trick already mentioned in the proof of [27, Proposition C.13].

Let $M=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . Suppose that $m_{1},m_{2}\in M$ are primitive, linearly independent, but may only generate a rank-2 proper sublattice $M^{\circ}\subsetneq M$ . The dual $N^{\circ}\coloneqq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M^{\circ},\mathbb{Z})$ naturally contains $N\coloneqq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ as a sublattice.

For any $m\in M$ , denote $m^{\perp}\coloneqq\{n\in N\otimes\mathbb{R}\mid n\cdot m=0\}$ . We define the index of $m$ to be

$$ \operatorname{ind}(m)\coloneqq|(m^{\perp}\cap N^{\circ})/(m^{\perp}\cap N)|, $$

that is, the order of the finite cyclic group $(m^{\perp}\cap N^{\circ})/(m^{\perp}\cap N)$ . For example, we have

$$ \operatorname{ind}(m_{1})=\operatorname{ind}(m_{2})=|M/M^{\circ}|\eqqcolon\ell. $$

Notice that $\operatorname{ind}(m)$ only depends on the line $\mathbb{R}m$ . We then define $\operatorname{ind}(\mathfrak{d})\coloneqq\mathrm{ind}(m_{\mathfrak{d}})$ , where $m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is the direction of either a ray or a line $\mathfrak{d}$ .

Take $\mathscr{P}=M\oplus\mathbb{M}$ to be the monoid in Section 2.2 with the projection $r\colon\mathscr{P}\rightarrow M$ . Let $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}=\{\mathfrak{d}_{1},\mathfrak{d}_{2}\}$ where

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=\mathbb{R}m_{i}\quad\text{and}\quad f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=f_{i}\coloneqq 1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,k}x^{km_{i}},\quad i=1,2. $$

By Theorem 2.10, we can assume that there is at most one added ray in $\mathfrak{D}$ with support $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(pm_{1}+qm_{2})$ for any positive coprime pair $(p,q)$ . Assuming that $m_{1},m_{2}$ form a basis of $M$ , we can express the attached wall-function as

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(pm_{1}+qm_{2})}=1+\sum_{d\geq 1}\lambda(dp,dq)x^{dpm_{1}+dqm_{2}}, $$

where $\lambda(dp,dq)\in\mathbb{N}[\mathbb{M}]$ is computed in Theorem 5.17.

#### Definition 9.3.

Define $\lambda(dp,dq;\ell)$ for coprime $(p,q)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}$ , $d\in\mathbb{N}$ , $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ by the following procedure. First we evaluate $\lambda(\ell dp,\ell dq)$ at $p_{i,k}=0$ for any $k$ not divisible by $\ell$ . Then we substitute any $p_{i,\ell k}$ by $p_{i,k}$ .

#### Example 9.4.

Let $(p,q)=(1,1)$ , $d=1$ , $\ell=2$ . For $\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=2$ , we compute $\lambda(1,1;2)$ . By Theorem 5.17, we have

$$ \lambda(2,2)=p_{1,1}^{2}p_{2,2}+p_{2,1}^{2}p_{1,2}+2p_{1,2}p_{2,2}. $$

After the evaluation at $p_{1,1}=p_{2,1}=0$ , we get $2p_{1,2}p_{2,2}$ . Substituting $p_{i,2}$ by $p_{i,1}$ , we obtain $\lambda(1,1;2)=2p_{1,1}p_{2,1}$ .

The following formula computes wall-functions in the non-standard case.

#### Theorem 9.5.

The wall-function in $\mathfrak{D}$ on any ray $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}$ with $m^{\circ}=pm_{1}+qm_{2}$ and $(p,q)$ positive coprime is

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}=\left(1+\sum_{d\geq 1}\lambda(dp,dq;\ell)x^{dpm_{1}+dqm_{2}}\right)^{\frac{\ell}{\mathrm{ind}(m^{\circ})}}. $$

where $\ell$ is defined in (9.1) and $\ell/\operatorname{ind}(m^{\circ})$ belongs to $\mathbb{N}$ . Hence every coefficient in the expansion of $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}$ is a polynomial in $p_{i,j}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{d}$ be a wall in $\mathfrak{D}$ . The associated wall-crossing automorphism is

$$ x^{m^{\prime}}\mapsto x^{m^{\prime}}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\pm n\cdot m^{\prime}}, $$

where $n$ is primitive in $N$ and orthogonal to $m_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . Notice that the index of $\mathfrak{d}$ is equivalently

$$ \mathrm{ind}(\mathfrak{d})\coloneqq\max\{d\in\mathbb{N}\mid n/d\in N^{\circ}\}. $$

Namely $n^{\circ}\coloneqq n/\mathrm{ind}(\mathfrak{d})$ is primitive in $N^{\circ}$ .

Consider the scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}^{\circ}\coloneqq\left\{\left(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\operatorname{ind}(\mathfrak{d})}\right)\,\middle|\,\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\right\}. $$

We claim that it is the consistent scattering diagram $\Scat(f_{1}^{\ell},f_{2}^{\ell})$ for the lattice $M^{\circ}$ . In fact, for $m^{\prime}\in M^{\circ}$ , the wall-crossing automorphism associated to $(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\operatorname{ind}(\mathfrak{d})})$ can be expressed as

$$ x^{m^{\prime}}\mapsto x^{m^{\prime}}\left(f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\mathrm{ind}(\mathfrak{d})}\right)^{\pm n^{\circ}\cdot m^{\prime}}=x^{m^{\prime}}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\pm n\cdot m^{\prime}} $$

where $n$ and $n^{\circ}$ are respectively the primitive normal vectors of $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ in $N$ and $N^{\circ}$ . It follows immediately that $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ is consistent because so is $\mathfrak{D}$ . Thus by the uniqueness, we have $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}=\Scat(f_{1}^{\ell},f_{2}^{\ell})$ .

In retrospect, we can use $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ to represent $\mathfrak{D}$ . This in particular implies that any wall-function $f$ of $\mathfrak{D}$ is always a power series of $x^{m^{\circ}}$ for some primitive $m^{\circ}$ in $M^{\circ}$ . Precisely, consider $(p,q)$ positive coprime and $m^{\circ}=pm_{1}+qm_{2}\in M^{\circ}$ . The wall-function $f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}$ in $\mathfrak{D}$ is then recovered by

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}=\left(f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}^{\circ}\right)^{\frac{1}{\mathrm{ind}(m^{\circ})}} $$

where $f^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}$ denotes the wall-function in $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ . This is not so ideal as taking the power of a fraction may break the integrality and the positivity.

However, we can change the lattice one more time. Consider the scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\Scat(f^{\prime}_{1},f^{\prime}_{2}) $$

again with respect to $M^{\circ}$ where for $i=1,2$

$$ f_{i}^{\prime}\coloneqq f_{i}(x^{\ell m_{i}})=1+\sum_{d\geq 1}p_{i,d}x^{\ell dm_{i}}. $$

For the ray with support $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}$ where $m^{\circ}=pm_{1}+qm_{2}$ for $(p,q)$ positive coprime, denote the wall-function by $f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}$ . By (9.2) and the substitution Definition 9.3, we have

$$ f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}=1+\sum_{d\geq 1}\lambda(dp,dq;\ell)x^{dpm_{1}+dqm_{2}}. $$

Now consider the wall-crossing automorphism associated to the above ray in $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ on $x^{a_{1}\ell m_{1}+a_{2}\ell m_{2}}$ with $a_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}$ :

$$ x^{a_{1}\ell m_{1}+a_{2}\ell m_{2}}\mapsto x^{a_{1}\ell m_{1}+a_{2}\ell m_{2}}(f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}})^{\pm\ell(pa_{2}-qa_{1})}. $$

Observe that these wall-crossings can be viewed as in a scattering diagram for $M^{\prime}$ generated by $\ell m_{1}$ and $\ell m_{2}$ . Therefore, by turning every $f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}$ into

$$ f^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}\coloneqq\left(f^{\prime}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}\mid x^{m_{i}}\leftarrow x^{\ell m_{i}}\right)^{\ell}, $$

we obtain a consistent scattering diagram for $M^{\circ}$ with the initial wall-functions $f_{1}^{\ell}$ and $f_{2}^{\ell}$ . By the uniqueness, this is exactly $\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}$ , hence justifying the previously defined notation $f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\circ}$ .

Now combining (9.6) with (9.7), the wall-function for $\mathfrak{D}$ can be recovered as

$$ f_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m^{\circ}}=\left(1+\sum_{d\geq 1}\lambda(dp,dq;\ell)x^{\ell d(pm_{1}+qm_{2})}\right)^{\frac{\ell}{\mathrm{ind}(m^{\circ})}}, $$

as stated in the theorem. Since for any $m\in M$ , we have

$$ \ell(m^{\perp}\cap N^{\circ})\subseteq m^{\perp}\cap N\subseteq m^{\perp}\cap N^{\circ}, $$

the index $\operatorname{ind}(m^{\circ})$ divides $\ell$ . ∎

#### Corollary 9.8.

Let $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}=\{\mathfrak{d}_{1},\mathfrak{d}_{2}\}$ be a scattering diagram of two lines, where

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=1+\sum_{m\in\mathscr{P}(m_{i})}c_{i,m}x^{m}\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]},\quad i=1,2. $$

Then there is a consistent scattering diagram in the equivalent class of $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})$ such that any coefficient $c_{m}\in\Bbbk$ of any wall-function

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=1+\sum_{m\in\mathscr{P}(m_{\mathfrak{d}})}c_{m}x^{m} $$

can be expressed as a polynomial in $\{c_{i,m}\mid i=1,2,m\in\mathscr{P}\}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients.

#### Proof.

Notice that we do not assume $\mathscr{P}=M\oplus\mathbb{M}$ and thus $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is not exactly of the form in Theorem 9.5. It suffices to show the positivity at each order $k\geq 1$ for $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k}$ . For fixed $k$ , we can choose large $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ and consider a close variant $\mathfrak{D}=\Scat(f_{1},f_{2})$ of the scattering diagram in Theorem 9.5 where

$$ f_{i}=1+\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{i}}p_{i,k}, $$

with the monoid $\mathbb{M}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ the monomials in $\{p_{i,k}\mid i=1,2,1\leq k\leq\ell_{i}\}$ equipped with $r^{\prime}\colon\mathbb{M}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}\rightarrow M$ such that $r^{\prime}(p_{i,k})=km_{i}$ . Then consider the algebra homomorphism

$$ \varphi\colon\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathbb{M}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}]}\rightarrow\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]},\quad\varphi(p_{i,k})=\sum_{r(m)=km_{i}}c_{i,m}x^{m}. $$

By the functoriality (2.11), we have $\varphi(\mathfrak{D})\equiv\Scat(\varphi(f_{1}),\varphi(f_{2}))$ . The positive integers $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ are sufficiently large so that $f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}\equiv\varphi(f_{i})\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ . Then the positivity of $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k}\equiv\varphi(\mathfrak{D})_{k}$ follows from that of $\mathfrak{D}$ by Theorem 9.5. ∎

### 9.2. Full positivity in rank 2

We now show that any rank-2 consistent scattering diagram is positive with respect to the initial coefficients.

Let $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}=\{\mathfrak{d}_{s}\mid s\in S\}$ be a scattering diagram (as defined in Section 2.1) of lines, where $S$ is a countable index set. We do not require the lines to pass through the origin. The initial wall-functions are expressed as

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}}=1+\sum_{m\in\mathscr{P}(m_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}})}c_{s,m}x^{m}\in\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}. $$

#### Theorem 9.9.

There exists a consistent scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ in the equivalent class of $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})$ such that any coefficient $c_{m}\in\Bbbk$ of any wall-function

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=1+\sum_{m\in\mathscr{P}}c_{m}x^{m} $$

can be expressed as a polynomial in $\{c_{s,m}\mid s\in S,m\in\mathscr{P}\}$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, which we call a positive polynomial.

#### Proof.

We prove by inductively constructing a finite scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ for each $k\geq 1$ such that $\mathfrak{D}_{k}\equiv\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k}$ and that the positivity holds for $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . This is clearly true for $k=1$ as we simply take $\mathfrak{D}_{1}=(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{1}$ . We add to the induction hypothesis that $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ is a union of $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k}$ and a set of rays such that no two rays have the same support.

Step 1: Reduction to the cone case.

We first reduce to the case where every initial line passes through the origin, which we refer to as the cone case.

For a singular point $p\in\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ , define

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}\mid p\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}. $$

When viewed as over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ , $\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)$ may fail to be consistent at $p$ . Translating the support of every wall in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)$ by $-p$ , we obtain a scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{loc}}(p)$ centered at the origin, which can be viewed as a local version of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)$ at $p$ . Denote the set of lines in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}^{\mathrm{loc}}(p)$ by $\mathfrak{D}_{k,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{loc}}(p)$ .

Assuming the inductive construction is valid in the cone case, we can modify $\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)$ as follows. We can add a finite collection $\mathfrak{D}_{k}[p]$ of new rays based at $p$ whose wall-functions are in $1+\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ and modify existing rays $\mathfrak{d}\mapsto\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}$ by only updating their wall-functions $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ by adding monomials in $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ where the coefficients of add terms are positive polynomials such that

$$ \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{k}(p)\coloneqq\mathfrak{D}_{k}[p]\cup\{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}\mid\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p),p=\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}\cup\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}(p)\mid p\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\cut\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}\} $$

is consistent at $p$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . Notice that this means $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{k}^{\mathrm{loc}}(p)\equiv\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{k,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{loc}}(p))\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ .

Globally, we construct

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k+1}\coloneqq(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k+1}\cup\bigcup_{p\,\in\,\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})}\left(\mathfrak{D}_{k}[p]\cup\{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}\mid\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k},\,p=\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}\right). $$

We show that the induction hypothesis holds for $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ .

Clearly $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is positive. To show $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}\equiv\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k+1}$ , it suffices to show the consistency for $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ because they share the same set of lines. Then we can check locally at each singular point $p\in\Sing(\mathfrak{D}_{k+1})$ . Suppose that $p\in\Sing(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ . For each $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}(p)$ such that $p\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\cut\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ , we write

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}}=f^{\prime}_{\mathfrak{d}}\cdot(1+\xi)\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}, $$

where $\xi$ is the part of $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ in $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\cut\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . The wall-crossing automorphism (and its inverse) associated to $1+\xi$ commutes with others modulo $\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . In the path-ordered product of a small loop around $p$ , such wall-crossing automorphism and its inverse both appear once and thus cancel out. Therefore to check the consistency at $p$ , we can replace $f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ with $f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{\prime}$ . After the replacement for every such $\mathfrak{d}$ , $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}(p)$ is equivalent to $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{k}(p)$ , hence consistent. A new singular point $p\in\Sing(\mathfrak{D}_{k+1})\cut\Sing(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ must be in the interior of some newly added ray. There is no ray based at $p$ . For consistency at $p$ , we can again ignore any newly added ray that contains $p$ in its interior. The rest walls containing $p$ are all in the same or the opposite direction, whose wall-crossing automorphisms commute and cancel out in the path-ordered product of a small loop around $p$ . Thus $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is consistent at $p$ .

Then the induction hypothesis is proven for $k+1$ by assuming that this can be done for the cone case.

Step 2: Perturbation trick.

We use the perturbation trick to handle the cone case. Choose for each $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ a sufficiently general vector $v_{\mathfrak{d}}\in M_{\mathbb{R}}$ and consider the perturbed scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{in}}$ with supports $S_{\mathfrak{d}}+v_{\mathfrak{d}}$ but the same wall-functions. After the perturbation, at most two initial lines intersect at any given point.

By the induction hypothesis, we have constructed positive $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{k}$ equivalent to $\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}^{\prime})_{k}$ , where $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{1}=(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{in}})_{1}$ . Because of the perturbation, for each $p\in\Sing(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{k})$ , there are at most two lines in $\left(\mathfrak{D}^{\prime,\mathrm{loc}}_{k,\mathrm{in}}(p)\right)_{1}$ , that is, at most two lines are non-trivial modulo $\mathfrak{m}^{2}$ . We want to show $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{k}(p)$ is positive at each $p$ . Notice that this is equivalent to show the induction hypothesis at $k+1$ for the initial scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime,\mathrm{loc}}_{k,\mathrm{in}}(p)$ . Once this is established, we can construct $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{k+1}$ as in Step 1. To get $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ , we then translate every wall in $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}_{k+1}$ back to pass through or based at the origin. Therefore it suffices to prove the induction step in the cone case with at most two non-trivial lines in $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{1}$

Step 3: Reduction to two initial lines.

By Step 2, we assume in the cone case that only $\mathfrak{d}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{d}_{2}$ are non-trivial in $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{1}$ . We may assume that $S=\{1,\dots,N\}$ since only finitely many initial lines are non-trivial up to a sufficiently large order. We want to show the induction hypothesis at $k+1$ , that is, on any ray in $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}=\Scat(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}})_{k+1}$ , every term $c_{p}x^{p}$ in $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\cut\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ has positive polynomial coefficient $c_{p}$ . Notice that

$$ p=\sum_{i,s}a_{i,s}p_{i,s} $$

for $a_{i,s}\in\mathbb{N}$ , where $p_{i,s}\in\mathscr{P}$ appears in $f_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}}$ . If any $a_{i,s}\neq 0$ for some $s\neq 1,2$ , then at most $k$ of $a_{i,s}$ are non-zero. The crucial point is that $c_{p}x^{p}$ can be viewed as a term of order at most $k$ after the change of monoid trick as follows. Express each $f_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}}$ as

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}}=1+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{s}}c_{i,s}x^{p_{i,s}}\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}. $$

Consider the monoid

$$ \mathbb{M}=\bigoplus_{s=1}^{N}\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell_{s}}\mathbb{N}\cdot e_{i,s} $$

with $r^{\prime}\colon\mathbb{M}\rightarrow M$ such that $r^{\prime}(e_{i,s})=r(p_{i,s})$ . Denote $\mathfrak{m}^{\prime}=\mathbb{M}\cut\{0\}$ . Consider the scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\Scat\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{s}}c_{i,s}x^{e_{i,s}}\,\middle|\,s=1,\dots,N\right). $$

By the functoriality (2.11), we can obtain $c_{p}x^{p}$ by a wall-function term $c_{p}x^{\sum_{i,s}a_{i,s}e_{i,s}}$ in $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ . Notice that now $\sum_{i,s}a_{i,s}e_{i,s}$ is in $(\mathfrak{m}^{\prime})^{j}\cut(\mathfrak{m}^{\prime})^{j+1}$ for some $j\leq k$ . So we apply the induction hypothesis at $k$ to this situation to conclude that $c_{p}$ is positive with respect to the initial coefficients.

Now we are left with $p$ as a linear combination of $p_{i,s}$ for $s=1,2$ only. Notice that these same terms appear in $\Scat(\mathfrak{d}_{1},\mathfrak{d}_{2})$ as one can simply let $x^{p_{i,s}}=0$ for $s\neq 1,2$ . Therefore we have reduced the problem to prove the induction hypothesis at $k+1$ for the case of two initial lines.

Step 4. When $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in}}$ only consists of two initial lines, the positivity follows immediately from Corollary 9.8.

Now the induction is complete. ∎

### 9.3. Positivity in higher ranks

We proceed to prove Theorem 8.11 the positivity of wall-functions in $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ as defined in Section 8.1. The strategy is to construct a sequence of scattering diagrams $(\mathfrak{D}_{k})_{k\geq 1}$ such that each $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ is over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ , has positive wall-functions, and is equivalent to $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k}$ .

We first realize the singular locus (8.7) of a finite scattering diagram as a cone complex. The support of each wall, as a polyhedral cone, is a finite intersection of closed linear half-spaces. Consider the collection of these half-spaces and their other halves from all the walls in $\mathfrak{D}$ . Some of their intersections are contained in $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ and $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ is a union of these intersections. They give rise to a cone complex structure on $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ .

#### Definition 9.10.

For any scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ of finitely many walls, the singular locus $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ can be realized as the union of the maximal cones of a cone complex of dimension $\dim M_{\mathbb{R}}-2$ such that for each such cone $\mathfrak{j}$ and $x\in\operatorname{Int}(\mathfrak{j})$ (the interior points of $\mathfrak{j}$ ), the set of walls

$$ \{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}\mid x\in S_{\mathfrak{d}}\} $$

is independent of $x$ . With such a realization, the maximal cones are called joints. In particular, any facet of $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is a union of joints with disjoint interiors.

The aforementioned cone complex structure on $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D})$ clearly satisfies the requirement in the above definition, thus giving a choice of joints.

Let $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ be $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}})_{1}$ . Concretely, the walls in $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}})_{1}$ are still $\mathfrak{d}_{i}$ for $i\in I_{\mathrm{uf}}$ with the support $S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=e_{i}^{\perp}$ and the wall-function

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=1+p_{i,1}x^{w_{i}}+\dots+p_{i,\ell_{i}}x^{\ell_{i}w_{i}} $$

because each monomial is in $\mathfrak{m}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{2}$ . It is consistent as the wall-crossing automorphisms commute over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{2}$ .

#### Example 9.11.

For $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ , we have

$$ \operatorname{Supp}(\mathfrak{D}_{1})=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}e_{i}^{\perp}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{1})=\bigcup_{i\neq j}e_{i}^{\perp}\cap e_{j}^{\perp}. $$

The joints of $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ are as follows. Let $H_{k}^{\varepsilon}$ for $\varepsilon\in\{+,-\}$ be the half space

$$ H_{k}^{\varepsilon}\coloneqq\{m\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\mid\mathrm{sgn}(\langle e_{k},m\rangle)=\varepsilon\}. $$

A joint is the closure of

$$ e_{i}^{\perp}\cap e_{j}^{\perp}\cap\bigcap_{k\neq i,j}H_{k}^{\varepsilon_{k}} $$

for $i\neq j$ and $\varepsilon_{k}\in\{+,-\}$ .

#### Definition 9.12.

A scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}$ is called consistent at a joint $\mathfrak{j}$ if the path-ordered product associated to a small loop around $\mathfrak{j}$ is identity. It is called consistent if it is consistent at each of its joint. This is equivalent to the previous definition in Section 8.1 where the consistency means the path-ordered product of any regular path only depends on the endpoints.

#### Remark 9.13.

By the definition of joints, the set of walls (whose support) containing a given joint is well-defined. There are two situations that a wall can contain a joint $\mathfrak{j}$ : (1) $\mathfrak{j}$ is contained in $\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ ; (2) $\mathrm{int}(\mathfrak{j})$ is contained in $\mathrm{int}(S_{\mathfrak{d}})$ . To check the consistency at $\mathfrak{j}$ , the small loop around $\mathfrak{j}$ is chosen to cross a wall of the first kind once and a wall of the second kind twice.

#### Lemma 9.14 ([27, Definition-Lemma C.2]).

Let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a finite scattering diagram as in Section 8.1. Let $\mathfrak{j}$ be a joint of $\mathfrak{D}$ . Then either every wall containing $\mathfrak{j}$ has direction tangent to $\mathfrak{j}$ or every wall containing $\mathfrak{j}$ has direction not tangent to $\mathfrak{j}$ . In the first case we call the joint parallel; in the second case, perpendicular.

Now we inductively construct for any $k\geq 1$ , a finite scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ to satisfy the following four assumptions.

- (A1) $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ is consistent over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ , that is, consistent at each joint.

- (A2) Any wall-function has positive coefficients, i.e., in $\mathbb{N}[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ .

- (A3) Any non-initial wall $\mathfrak{d}$ is outgoing and always has support of the form

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}}=F_{\mathfrak{d}}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}}) $$

where $F_{\mathfrak{d}}\subseteq\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is a facet. In particular, $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is the only facet not tangent to the direction of $\mathfrak{d}$ . We say that $\mathfrak{d}$ or $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is based at $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ .

- (A4) Any perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}$ is contained in the facet of at most one outgoing wall in each possible direction.

The base case $\mathfrak{D}_{1}$ clearly satisfies all four assumptions.

Now we construct $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ by essentially modifying existing walls in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ and adding new walls based at perpendicular joints of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . Precisely, the construction comprises three steps.

Step 1: subdivision of outgoing walls.

By the assumption (A3), every outgoing wall $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ has support

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}}=F_{\mathfrak{d}}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}}) $$

where $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ is a facet not tangent to $\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}})$ . Being in the boundary of $S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ , the facet $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ inherits part of the cone complex realization of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ . Thus we can subdivide $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ into joints

$$ F_{\mathfrak{d}}=\mathfrak{j}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mathfrak{j}_{s}. $$

Note that these joints are all perpendicular. Accordingly $\mathfrak{d}$ is subdivided into walls $\mathfrak{d}_{1},\dots,\mathfrak{d}_{s}$ with smaller supports

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}_{1}}=\mathfrak{j}_{1}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}}),\dots,S_{\mathfrak{d}s}=\mathfrak{j}_{s}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}}), $$

and with wall-functions

$$ f_{\mathfrak{d}_{1}}=\dots=f_{\mathfrak{d}_{s}}=f_{\mathfrak{d}}. $$

We replace $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ with an equivalent scattering diagram by implementing the above subdivision on every outgoing wall. Clearly it still satisfies the four assumptions. The set of joints remains unchanged. We also note that an initial wall never gets subdivided as it is incoming.

Step 2: rank-2 scattering at perpendicular joints.

Consider at each perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ the scattering diagram

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}\mid\mathfrak{j}\subseteq S_{\mathfrak{d}}\}, $$

that is, the collection of walls whose support contains $\mathfrak{j}$ . Let $\Lambda_{\mathfrak{j}}$ denote the tangent space of (any interior point of) $\mathfrak{j}$ . It can thus be viewed as a $(\dim M_{\mathbb{R}}-2)$ -dimensional subspace of $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ . We next construct a rank-2 scattering diagram $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ with respect to the lattice

$$ M_{\mathfrak{j}}\coloneqq\omega(-,\Lambda_{\mathfrak{j}}^{\perp})\cap M, $$

living in the subspace $M_{\mathfrak{j},\mathbb{R}}\coloneqq\omega(-,\Lambda_{\mathfrak{j}}^{\perp})\subseteq M_{\mathbb{R}}$ . These are of rank $2$ because of the injectivity assumption on the form $\omega(-,-)$ .

The monoid for $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ is

$$ \mathscr{P}_{\mathfrak{j}}\coloneqq\{p\in\mathscr{P}\mid r(p)\in M_{\mathfrak{j}}\}=M_{\mathfrak{j}}\oplus\mathbb{P}^{\oplus}=M_{\mathfrak{j}}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{|I_{\mathrm{uf}}|}\mathbb{N}^{\ell_{i}}. $$

Let $\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ denote $\mathscr{P}_{\mathfrak{j}}\setminus\mathscr{P}_{\mathfrak{j}}^{\times}$ as well as the corresponding monomial ideal in $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{\mathfrak{j}}]$ . For each $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ , define a wall $\overline{\mathfrak{d}}$ with the support

$$ S_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}\coloneqq S_{\mathfrak{d}}\cap M_{\mathfrak{j},\mathbb{R}} $$

and the wall-function $f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}\coloneqq f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . Clearly by the particular form of the wall-function, the direction of $\overline{\mathfrak{d}}$ is $m_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}=m_{\mathfrak{d}}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}})\cap M$ where $n_{\mathfrak{d}}\in N^{+}$ is the normal vector of $\mathfrak{d}$ . One should carefully check that when $S_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ is a ray, it must be of the form $\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}m_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ instead of $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}m_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ . By the assumption (A3), this is indeed the case.

Now we define the scattering diagram

$$ \overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}\coloneqq\{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}\mid\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}\}. $$

The walls in this rank-2 scattering diagram are either lines or rays. By the assumption (A4), rays are in distinct directions (but may overlap with lines).

We then take the consistent completion $\Scat(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}})$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}_{\mathfrak{j}}]/\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{j}}^{k+2}$ . This is equivalent to the consistent completion of only lines in $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ , as studied in Section 9.2. Notice that $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ is already consistent over $\Bbbk[P_{\mathfrak{j}}]/{\mathfrak{m}}_{\mathfrak{j}}^{k+1}$ because by (A1) $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ is consistent at $\mathfrak{j}$ . Therefore, by the positivity Theorem 9.9 we can obtain a representative of $\Scat(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}})$ by

- (1) adding new rays $\mathfrak{d}(n_{0})$ with support $S_{\mathfrak{d}(n_{0})}=\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{0})$ and wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}(n_{0})}$ with only non-trivial monomial terms in $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ with positive integer coefficients for distinct $n_{0}\in\Lambda_{\mathfrak{j}}^{\perp}\cap N^{+}$ ;

- (2) for any existing ray $\overline{\mathfrak{d}}$ in $\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ , adding positive terms in $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ to $f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ (and calling it $f^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ ).

The crucial point here is that the positivity is guaranteed by Theorem 9.9.

Step 3: constructing $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ .

For each new ray added in (1), define a wall in $M_{\mathbb{R}}$ with the support

$$ \mathfrak{j}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{0}) $$

and the same wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}(n_{0})}$ . Since $\mathfrak{j}$ is perpendicular, such a wall is outgoing as the support must not contain $\omega(-,n_{0})$ . Denote this (finite) collection of walls by $\mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})$ .

Now we define

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k+1}\coloneqq(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}\cup\bigcup_{\mathfrak{j}}\left(\mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})\cup\{(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}})\mid\mathfrak{j}\subseteq\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}},\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}\}\right), $$

where $\bigcup_{\mathfrak{j}}$ is over all perpendicular joints in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . We note that each existing outgoing $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ appears exactly once in the union because it only contains a unique perpendicular joint after the subdivision in Step 1. We have finished the construction of $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ .

We next elaborate on why $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ satisfies assumptions (A2) to (A4). We then discuss the consistency assumption (A1), which will be proven in Lemma 9.16.

For (A2), as pointed out earlier, the positivity is preserved by Theorem 9.9. Any wall in $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ (except the initial ones) is either in some $\mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})$ or of the form $(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}^{\prime})$ arising from some $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}$ such that $\mathfrak{j}\subseteq\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . Clearly both kinds are outgoing. Any such $\mathfrak{d}$ has support of the form

$$ \mathfrak{j}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}}) $$

where $\mathfrak{j}$ is regarded as $F_{\mathfrak{d}}$ . So (A3) is satisfied by $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ .

The statement of (A4) involves joints in $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ upon a cone complex realization of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k+1})$ . Since $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k+1})$ contains $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ , we can require that the cone complex of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k+1})$ , when restricted on $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ , is a refinement of the cone complex of $\operatorname{Sing}(\mathfrak{D}_{k})$ . We then have the following two cases for any perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ in $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ .

Case 1. Suppose that $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in a perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . Notice that the outgoing walls in $\mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})$ and the outgoing walls of the form $(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}})$ are all in distinct directions. Thus we only need to show if there is a wall $\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ based at another perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}_{1}$ (of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ ) such that $S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}$ contains $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ , the only case can happen is

$$ \mathrm{int}(\mathfrak{j}^{\prime})\subseteq\mathrm{int}(S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}). $$

Otherwise assume that $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in $\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}$ . Notice that we have

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}=\mathfrak{j}_{1}+\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}}), $$

where $\mathfrak{j}_{1}$ is the only facet not tangent to the direction $\omega(-,n_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}})$ . Thus $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in $\mathfrak{j}_{1}$ . Then $\mathfrak{j}_{1}$ and $\mathfrak{j}$ (both as joints of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ ) have maximal dimensional intersection, a contradiction.

Case 2. Suppose that $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is not contained in any perpendicular joint of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . Assume that $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in a facet of a wall $\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ . Then it must be contained in the only possible facet that is not tangent to the direction. However, such a facet is always a perpendicular joint of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ , a contradiction. This argument also implies that any such perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is not in the boundary of any wall.

#### Lemma 9.15.

$\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is consistent at each perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ .

#### Proof.

The analysis proceeds by considering the same two cases on whether $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in a perpendicular joint $\mathfrak{j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ , as when we show (A4).

When $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is contained in some perpendicular $\mathfrak{j}$ of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ , we check all walls $\mathfrak{d}$ containing $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ , namely the scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}}$ . The idea is then to derive the consistency of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}}$ from $\Scat(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}})$ . There are two kinds of $\mathfrak{d}$ :

$$ \mathfrak{j}^{\prime}\subseteq\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}}\quad\text{or}\quad\mathrm{int}(\mathfrak{j}^{\prime})\subseteq\mathrm{int}(S_{\mathfrak{d}}). $$

The walls of the first kind are exactly those in

$$ \mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})\cup\{(S_{\mathfrak{d}},f^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}})\mid\mathfrak{j}\subseteq\partial S_{\mathfrak{d}},\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}}\}. $$

For the second kind, we can get rid of those whose wall-functions are purely in order $k+1$ since their wall-crossing automorphisms commute with others over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . The remaining walls of the second kind are from walls in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . The possible difference on the wall-function is only in order $k+1$ , as mentioned in the construction, namely $f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}^{\prime}$ versus $f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ . Notice that

$$ f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}^{\prime}=f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}\cdot(1+f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}^{\prime}-f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}})\mod\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}. $$

The wall-crossing automorphism associated to the function $1+f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}^{\prime}-f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ commute with others over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . Therefore, we can replace $f^{\prime}_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}$ with $f_{\overline{\mathfrak{d}}}=f_{\mathfrak{d}}$ and such a wall rolls back to the version in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . Now we see that the consistency of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}}$ is equivalent to that of $\Scat(\overline{\mathfrak{D}}_{\mathfrak{j}})$ .

The case where $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is not contained in any perpendicular joint of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ is simpler. We have understood that $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is not in the boundary of any wall. Such a joint is created only because of the intersection with new walls, i.e., the ones in $\mathfrak{D}(\mathfrak{j})$ for some $\mathfrak{j}$ . Those walls always contain $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ of the form

$$ \mathrm{int}(\mathfrak{j}^{\prime})\subseteq\mathrm{int}(S_{\mathfrak{d}}). $$

Thus as argued earlier, we can get rid of those walls and are left with only existing walls in $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ containing $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ . The only possibility is that the walls

$$ \{\mathfrak{d}\in\mathfrak{D}_{k}\mid\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}\subseteq S_{\mathfrak{d}}\} $$

are all in the same direction; otherwise $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ would have been in a perpendicular joint of $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ . Since $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is not in the boundary of any wall, these walls all pass through $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ . The consistency around $\mathfrak{j}^{\prime}$ is then clear. ∎

We apply Lemma 9.15 to show

#### Lemma 9.16.

$\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is consistent over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ .

#### Proof.

The strategy is to compare $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ with $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ and to show they are equivalent. The scattering diagram $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ is over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ , consistent and contains finitely many outgoing walls besides the initial walls. We note that the existence of $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ does not depend on the constructive process described here. See Theorem 8.9 and also [27, Theorem 1.21], which are both incarnation of [34, Theorem 2.1.6].

Firstly, these two scattering diagrams are equivalent over $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ , for they are consistent and share the same collection of incoming walls. It is convenient to consider their difference $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ , as a scattering diagram. In fact, one can subdivide walls in $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ and $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ and add walls with trivial wall-functions so that they have walls labeled by the same index set $S$

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{k+1}=\{\mathfrak{d}_{i}\mid i\in S\}\quad\text{and}\quad(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}=\{\mathfrak{c}_{i}\mid i\in S\} $$

such that $S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}=S_{\mathfrak{c}_{i}}$ for every $i\in S$ . Their difference is $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}=\{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}_{i}\mid i\in S\}$ where

$$ S_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}_{i}}\coloneqq S_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}\quad\text{and}\quad f_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}_{i}}\coloneqq f_{\mathfrak{d}_{i}}\cdot f_{\mathfrak{c}_{i}}^{-1}. $$

The wall-function $f_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}_{i}}$ must be of the form $1+\xi$ where $\xi\in\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ since it is trivial modulo $\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ .

Take another representative of $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ such that there are only non-trivial walls and they intersect only at codimension two. Notice that in this representative, walls are all outgoing since both $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ and $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ have the exact same collection of incoming walls.

Assume that there are non-trivial walls in a hyperplane $n_{0}^{\perp}$ . Let $\mathfrak{j}$ be a joint (for $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ ) in $n_{0}^{\perp}$ . If it is not tangent to $\omega(-,n_{0})$ , we claim that there are walls in $n_{0}^{\perp}$ on both sides of $\mathfrak{j}$ with the same wall-function. In fact, by Lemma 9.15, $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ is consistent at every perpendicular joint modulo $\mathfrak{m}^{k+2}$ . Hence $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is also consistent at $\mathfrak{j}$ (as $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ is consistent overall). Since the wall-crossing automorphisms associated to those $f_{\mathfrak{d}^{\prime}_{i}}$ all commute, the claim follows. Now take the union $U$ (which is a polyhedral cone but not necessarily convex) of all walls in $n_{0}^{\perp}$ . Each facet of $U$ is tangent to $\omega(-,n_{0})$ . This forces the whole line $\mathbb{R}\omega(-,n_{0})$ to lie in the boundary of $U$ , giving the presence of a non-trivial incoming wall in $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ , a contradiction. We can then conclude that $\mathfrak{D}^{\prime}$ is trivial and therefore $\mathfrak{D}_{k+1}$ and $(\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}})_{k+1}$ are equivalent. ∎

Now we have obtained a sequence $(\mathfrak{D}_{k})_{k\geq 1}$ of consistent scattering diagram over $\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}$ with finitely many walls without any incoming walls besides the initials. For the final step, we ensure that the limit when $k\rightarrow\infty$ exists as a scattering diagram over $\widehat{\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}]}$ . Notice that in this order by order construction, we either add a new outgoing wall or add higher order terms to the wall-function of an existing outgoing wall. The limit $\mathfrak{D}_{\infty}$ is taken to consist of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathrm{in},\mathbf{s}}$ and any outgoing wall that first appears in some $\mathfrak{D}_{k}$ with the wall-function being the limit of the wall-functions on the (support of the) same wall in $\mathfrak{D}_{i}$ , $i\geq k$ . Evidently for each $k\geq 1$ we have

$$ \left(\mathfrak{D}_{\infty}\right)_{k}=\mathfrak{D}_{k}. $$

It follows that $\mathfrak{D}_{\infty}$ is consistent and has every wall-function in $\widehat{\mathbb{N}[\mathscr{P}]}$ . By the uniqueness in Theorem 8.9, $\mathfrak{D}_{\infty}$ is equivalent to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathbf{s}}$ . This is the end of the proof of Theorem 8.11.

## Appendix A Proof of the generalized greedy element formula

In this appendix, we prove the expansion formula for generalized greedy elements in terms of compatible gradings given by Theorem 3.18. The majority of the proof closely follows that of [51, Theorem 2.15], and we discuss only those portions that require modification here. Namely, we generalize some of the necessary lemmas to the case where $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are not necessarily palindromic.

### A.1. Cluster variables up to a scalar

Recall the notations in Section 2.2 and the definition of cluster variables $x_{i}$ from Definition 2.35. We define elements $\{\widetilde{x}_{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}\}\subseteq\mathcal{F}=\operatorname{Frac}(\Bbbk[\mathscr{P}])$ and will show $x_{k}/\widetilde{x}_{k}\in\mathbb{P}$ . These scaled cluster variables will be convenient for our proofs in Sections A.2 and A.3.

Let $\widetilde{x}_{1}=x_{1}$ and $\widetilde{x}_{2}=x_{2}$ . We inductively define $\widetilde{x}_{k}\in\mathcal{F}$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ by the rule:

$$ \widetilde{x}_{k+1}\widetilde{x}_{k-1}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{k})&\text{if }k\equiv 1\mod 4,\\
P_{2}(\widetilde{x}_{k})&\text{if }k\equiv 2\mod 4,\\
\overline{P}_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{k})&\text{if }k\equiv 3\mod 4,\\
\overline{P}_{2}(\widetilde{x}_{k})&\text{if }k\equiv 0\mod 4.\\
\end{array}\right. $$

#### Lemma A.1.

For any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the quotient $x_{k}/\widetilde{x}_{k}$ is a Laurent monomial in $p_{1,\ell_{1}}$ and $p_{2,\ell_{2}}$ . More precisely, we have

$$ x_{k}/\widetilde{x}_{k}=\begin{cases}W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}-e_{2})\quad\text{if $k\equiv 0\mod 4$},\\
W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{1})\quad\text{if $k\equiv 1\mod 4$},\\
W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{2})\quad\text{if $k\equiv 2\mod 4$},\\
W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}-e_{1})\quad\text{if $k\equiv 3\mod 4$}.\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that $x_{k}/W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}\pm e_{i})$ satisfy the exchange relations of $\widetilde{x}_{k}$ . We check for $k\equiv 1\mod 4$ the following relation and the remaining cases are similar. Notice that by Lemma 2.36, we have

$$ \displaystyle x_{k-1}x_{k+1} \displaystyle=\bar{\zeta}_{n}(x_{k})=\frac{W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{1})^{\ell_{1}}}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}}P_{1}(x_{k}/W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{1})), \displaystyle\widetilde{x}_{k-1}\widetilde{x}_{k+1} \displaystyle=\frac{W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{1})^{\ell_{1}}}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}W({\mathbf{d}}_{k-1}-e_{2})W({\mathbf{d}}_{k+1}+e_{2})}P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{k}). $$

Now the desired relation follows from $W({\mathbf{d}}_{k}+e_{1})^{\ell_{1}}=p_{1,\ell_{1}}W({\mathbf{d}}_{k-1}-e_{2})W({\mathbf{d}}_{k+1}+e_{2})$ , which is result of

$$ {\mathbf{d}}_{k-1}+{\mathbf{d}}_{k+1}=\ell_{1}{\mathbf{d}}_{k}\,.\qed $$

### A.2. The strong Laurent phenomenon

We begin by establishing the strong Laurent phenomenon for the rank- $2$ generalized cluster algebras $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ , which is the $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ -subalgebra of $\mathcal{F}$ generated by all scaled cluster variables $\widetilde{x}_{k}$ . By Lemma A.1, this notion coincides with the $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ defined in Section 2.4.

#### Theorem A.2 (following [51, Theorem 2.2]).

For any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})=\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]\,. $$

#### Proof.

By Lemma A.1, it is enough to work with cluster pre-variables instead of cluster variables. We show via induction on $m$ that $\widetilde{x}_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]$ , hence $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})\subseteq\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]$ . Consider the element $\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+4}$ , where without loss of generality we assume $m\equiv 2\mod 4$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{x}_{m}-\frac{\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+4}}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}} \displaystyle=p_{1,\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m}-\frac{\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}}P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m+3})}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}} \displaystyle=\widetilde{x}_{m}-\frac{\overline{P_{1}}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1})}{\widetilde{x}_{m+2}}+\frac{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1})-\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}}P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m+3})}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}} \displaystyle=\frac{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1})-\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}}P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m+3})}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{\ell_{1}}p_{1,t}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m+3}^{t}-1)\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}-t}}{p_{1,\ell_{1}}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}}\,. $$

Using that $\overline{P_{2}}$ has constant term $1$ , we have $\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m+3}^{t}-1=(\overline{P_{2}}(\widetilde{x}_{m+2}))^{t}-1\in\widetilde{x}_{m+2}\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m+2}]$ for every $t\geq 0$ . Thus,

$$ \frac{\sum_{t=0}^{\ell_{1}}p_{1,t}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m+3}^{t}-1)\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{\ell_{1}-t}}{\widetilde{x}_{m+2}}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m+1},x_{m+2}]\,. $$

We then can see that $\widetilde{x}_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m+1},x_{m+2},x_{m+3},x_{m+4}]$ , and using a similar argument we obtain $\widetilde{x}_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-4},x_{m-3},x_{m-2},x_{m-1}]$ . We can then conclude that

$$ \widetilde{x}_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{k} $$

for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Since we have by definition that $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]\subseteq\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ , the desired equality follows. ∎

We now show that the cluster algebra $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ equals the corresponding upper cluster algebra $\mathcal{U}$ , as defined in Section 2.4, and moreover that it is the intersection of the Laurent polynomial ring of three consecutive clusters.

#### Theorem A.3 (Strong Laurent Phenomenon, following [51, Theorem 2.5]).

For any $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ we have

$$ \mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})=\bigcap_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{T}_{k}=\bigcap_{k=m-1}^{m+1}\mathcal{T}_{k}\,. $$

#### Proof.

By Theorem A.2, it is enough to show that

$$ \mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]=\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}\,. $$

The containment of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]$ into $\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}$ follows from Proposition 2.38. We show the other containment by taking the decomposition

$$ \mathcal{T}_{m}=\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1}^{\pm 1}]+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][\widetilde{x}_{m}^{\pm 1},\widetilde{x}_{m+1}] $$

and proving containment of the intersection of each summand with $\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}$ .

We begin by establishing the following:

$$ \mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}=\begin{cases}\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]&\text{ if }\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\geq 2\\
\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}]&\text{ if }\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=1\\
\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m-1}^{\ell_{2}}x_{m+2}]&\text{ if }\ell_{1}=0\\
\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}^{\ell_{1}},x_{m+2}]&\text{ if $\ell_{2}=0$}\end{cases} $$

Without loss of generality, we assume $m\equiv 1\mod 4$ . In order to simplify the exchange relations, we often work with the scaled cluster pre-variables rather than cluster variables due to Lemma A.1.

We first show that the ring on the right of (A.4) is contained in the intersection on the left of (A.4). By Proposition 2.38, each ring on the right is contained in $\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}$ , so it remains to show containment in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]$ . This containment is clear for $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\geq 2$ . When $\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=1$ , we have

$$ \widetilde{x}_{m-1}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}=P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m})\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1}P_{2}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1})\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]\,. $$

When $\ell_{1}=0$ or $\ell_{2}=0$ , where without loss of generality we assume the former, we have $\widetilde{x}_{m-1}=\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1}$ and

$$ \widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{\ell_{2}}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}=\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-\ell_{2}}P_{2}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1})\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1}=p_{2,\ell_{2}}\overline{P_{2}}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1})\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]\,. $$

In each of these cases, we can now readily see that the generators of the ring on the right of (A.4) are contained in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]$ .

We now handle the other containment of (A.4) case-by-case. Consider $y\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]$ , and express $y$ as

$$ y=\sum_{s,t\geq 0}c_{s,t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-s}\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-t}\,, $$

with finitely many nonzero coefficients $c_{s,t}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ . We then have

$$ y=\sum_{t\geq 0}\frac{\sum_{s\geq 0}c_{s,t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-s}}{P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}=\sum_{t\geq 0}\frac{\sum_{s\geq 0}c_{s,t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-s}}{\overline{P_{1}}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{\ell_{1}t}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}\,. $$

If $y\in\mathcal{T}_{m-1}$ , then for all $t\geq 0$ we have $\frac{\sum_{s\geq 0}c_{s,t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-s}}{\overline{P_{1}}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{t}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1}]$ , where we denote this polynomial by $C_{t}(x_{m}^{-1})$ . So we can now express $y$ as

$$ \displaystyle y \displaystyle=\sum_{t\geq 0}C_{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-\ell_{1}t}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t} \displaystyle=\sum_{t\geq 0}C_{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m})^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-\ell_{1}t}\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-t} \displaystyle=\sum_{t\geq 0}C_{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{t}\overline{P_{1}}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1})\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-t}\,. $$

Similarly, if $y\in\mathcal{T}_{m+1}$ , we have

$$ y=\sum_{t\geq 0}C^{\prime}_{s}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1})\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-\ell_{2}s}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}^{s}=\sum_{t\geq 0}C^{\prime}_{s}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1})p_{2,\ell_{2}}^{s}\overline{P_{2}}^{s}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1})\widetilde{x}_{m}^{s} $$

for some polynomials $C_{s}^{\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{-1})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m+1}^{-1}]$ .

From this point, the proof follows essentially verbatim from Rupel’s work [51, Theorem 2.5], but we include the remainder of the argument here for completeness.

If $d_{2}=0$ , then $\widetilde{x}_{m}^{-1}=\widetilde{x}_{m+2}$ and (A.5) becomes

$$ y=\sum_{t\geq 0}C_{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m+2})\widetilde{x}_{m+2}^{\ell_{1}t}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}^{\ell_{1}},x_{m+2}]\,. $$

Similarly, if $d_{1}=0$ then

$$ y=\sum_{s\geq 0}C_{s}^{\prime}(\widetilde{x}_{m-1})\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{\ell_{2}s}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}^{s}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m-1}^{\ell_{2}}x_{m+2}]\,. $$

We now consider when $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\neq 0$ . Let $\sigma(t)$ be maximal such that $c_{\sigma(t),t}\neq 0$ , and using the last equality in (A.5) we must have $\sigma(t)\geq\ell_{1}t$ . Similarly, let $\tau(s)$ maximal such that $c_{s,\tau(s)}\neq 0$ , and we have $\tau(s)\geq\ell_{2}s$ .

Suppose $t$ is maximal such that $c_{s,t}\neq 0$ for some choice of $s$ . Then $c_{\sigma(t),\tau(\sigma(t)))}\neq 0$ , and $\tau(\sigma(t))\geq\ell_{2}\sigma(t)\geq\ell_{1}\ell_{2}t$ . For $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\geq 2$ and $t>0$ this implies $\tau(\sigma(t))>t$ , which contradicts the maximality of $t$ . Thus we must have $t=0$ and, similarly, $s=0$ when $\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\geq 2$ . Hence $y\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}]$ .

Now suppose $\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=1$ . Then we have $\tau(\sigma(t))\geq\sigma(t)\geq t$ , and by the maximality of $t$ these are equalities. Using induction on the maximal value $t$ such that $c_{t,t}\neq 0$ , we can see that $y\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}]$ . The base case $t=0$ is clear. When $t>0$ , the element $y-c_{t,t}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}\widetilde{x}_{m+2}^{t}$ is contained in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}]$ , hence $y$ is also contained in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1}x_{m+2}]$ . Thus (A.4) is proved.

It then remains to show the equality

$$ \mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1}^{\pm 1}]=\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m},x_{m+1}]\subset\mathcal{T}_{m+1}\,. $$

The inclusion of $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m},x_{m+1}]$ into $\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1}^{\pm 1}]$ is clear. For the other inclusion, note that any $y\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1}^{\pm 1}]$ can be written in the form

$$ y=\sum_{t=-N}^{N}c_{t}x_{m+2}^{t} $$

for some positive integer $N$ and coefficients $c_{t}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}]$ . We then have

$$ y=\sum_{t=0}^{N}c_{t}P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{-t}+\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{c_{-t}}{P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}\,. $$

If $y\in\mathcal{T}_{m-1}$ , then we must have $\frac{c_{-t}}{P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{\pm 1}]$ for all $1\leq t\leq N$ . Since $P_{1}(\widetilde{x}_{m})$ has constant term $1$ , this implies $\frac{c_{-t}}{P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}]$ . Thus we have

$$ y=\sum_{t=0}^{N}c_{t}\widetilde{x}_{m+1}^{t}+\sum_{t=1}^{N}\frac{c_{-t}}{P_{1}^{t}(\widetilde{x}_{m})}\widetilde{x}_{m-1}^{t}\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m},x_{m+1}]\,. $$

We can similarly obtain $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{\pm 1},x_{m+1}]\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}=\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1},x_{m+2}]\subset\mathcal{T}_{m-1}$ . Combining these inclusions yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m}\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1} \displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\left(\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1}^{\pm 1}]+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{\pm 1},x_{m+1}]\right)\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1} \displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{m-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m}^{-1},x_{m+1}^{-1}]\cap\mathcal{T}_{m+1}+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m-1},x_{m},x_{m+1}] \displaystyle\qquad+\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{m},x_{m+1},x_{m+2}] \displaystyle\subset\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{P}][x_{k-1},x_{k},x_{k+1},x_{k+2}]\,, $$

as desired. ∎

### A.3. Proof of the compatible grading formula

This section closely follows the approach of Rupel in [51], with necessary adjustments made to extend the argument to the case when $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are not palindromic. In the compatible grading formula given by Theorem 3.18, the horizontal edges of the Dyck path are weighted by the coefficients of $P_{2}$ and the vertical edges are weighted by the coefficients of $P_{1}$ . We introduce auxiliary variants of this weighting, replacing $P_{i}$ with $\overline{P_{i}}$ .

#### Definition A.7.

For a grading $\omega:E(d_{1},d_{2})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , we define

$$ \displaystyle\text{wt}^{\prime}(\omega) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{d_{1}}p_{2,\ell_{2}-\omega(u_{i})}\prod_{j=1}^{d_{2}}p_{1,\omega(v_{j})}\in\Bbbk[\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{1}}\oplus\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{2}}]\,,\text{ and} \displaystyle\text{wt}^{\prime\prime}(\omega) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{d_{1}}p_{2,\omega(u_{i})}\prod_{j=1}^{d_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}-\omega(v_{j})}\in\Bbbk[\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{1}}\oplus\mathbb{Z}^{\ell_{2}}]\,. $$

We need to introduce the following auxiliary variants of the generalized greedy elements.

#### Definition A.8.

We define $x^{\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]\coloneqq x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{(S_{1},S_{2})}\wt^{\prime}(\omega)x_{1}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}$ , and similarly let $x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]\coloneqq x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{(S_{1},S_{2})}\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)x_{1}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}$ .

We now consider two automorphisms of the field of rational functions $\mathcal{F}$ . These maps are defined by their behavior on a generating set and given by $\sigma_{1}:(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto(x_{1},x_{0})$ and $\sigma_{2}:(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto(x_{3},x_{2})$ . In the case that $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ are palindromic, these are the usual reflection automorphisms $\sigma_{j}$ , where $\sigma_{j}(x_{m})=x_{2j-m}$ . We show that applying these automorphisms to a varient of some generalized greedy element results in a “mutated” generalized greedy element.

#### Proposition A.9 (following [51, Proposition 2.17]).

For any $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ the elements $x[d_{1},d_{2}]$ defined by (3.19) satisfy

$$ \sigma_{1}(x^{\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}])=x[d_{1},\ell_{1}[d_{1}]_{+}-d_{2}]\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\sigma_{2}(x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}])=x[\ell_{2}[d_{2}]_{+}-d_{1},d_{2}]\,. $$

#### Proof.

By symmetry, it is enough to establish the second identity. We do so by handling several cases.

First, suppose $d_{1},d_{2}\leq 0$ . Then $\mathcal{P}([d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+})=\mathcal{P}(0,0)$ is a single point, so we have

$$ \sigma_{2}(x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}])=\sigma_{2}(x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}})=x_{3}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}=x_{1}^{d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{-d_{1}}\,. $$

We can also directly compute $x[\ell_{2}[d_{2}]_{+}-d_{1},d_{2}]=x[-d_{1},d_{2}]$ using Theorem 3.18. Since $\mathcal{P}_{[-d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+}}=\mathcal{P}_{-d_{1},0}$ , we have $x[-d_{1},d_{2}]=x_{1}^{d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{-d_{1}}$ , as desired.

Next, suppose $d_{1}\leq 0<d_{2}$ . Then $\mathcal{P}([d_{1}]_{+},[d_{2}]_{+})$ consists of $d_{2}$ vertical edges. Similar to the previous case, we have $x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]=x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{d_{2}}\overline{P_{1}}(x_{1})^{d_{2}}$ . Applying $\sigma_{2}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{2}(x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]) \displaystyle=x_{3}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{d_{2}}\overline{P_{1}}(x_{3})^{d_{2}} \displaystyle=x_{1}^{d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{d_{2}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{-d_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(P_{2}(x_{2})x_{1}^{-1})^{d_{2}} $$

Note that every vertical edge in $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_{2}a_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}}$ has at least $\ell_{2}$ vertical edges in front of it. Thus any compatible grading with vertical weights bounded by $\ell_{2}$ can be constructed by taking a set of vertical edges and any horizontal edges not contained in the shadow of the vertical edges. Focusing just a vertical edge and the edges in its shadow, which is identical to $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_{2},1}$ , we can see that

$$ \sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}_{\ell_{2},1}}\wt(\omega)x_{1}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}=p_{1,\ell_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(P_{2}(x_{2})x_{1}^{-1})x_{1}^{\ell_{2}}\,. $$

We can view compatible gradings on $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}}$ as a collection of $d_{2}$ compatible gradings on $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_{2},1}$ along with compatible gradings on $-d_{1}$ additional horizontal edges. So, using the compatible grading definition, we have

$$ \displaystyle x[\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}] \displaystyle=x_{1}^{-\ell_{2}d_{2}+d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\left(p_{1,\ell_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(P_{2}(x_{2})x_{1}^{-1})\right)^{d_{2}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{-d_{1}} \displaystyle=x_{1}^{d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}p_{1,\ell_{1}}^{d_{2}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{-d_{1}}\overline{P_{1}}(P_{2}(x_{2})x_{1}^{-1})^{d_{2}}\,. $$

Lastly, suppose $0<d_{1},d_{2}$ . Then we have $\displaystyle x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]=x_{1}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)x_{1}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{2}(x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]) \displaystyle=x_{3}^{-d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)x_{3}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})} \displaystyle=x_{1}^{-\ell_{2}d_{2}+d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)x_{1}^{\ell_{2}d_{2}-\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}P_{2}(x_{2})^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})-d_{1}}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}\,. $$

Let $\mathcal{C}^{\sh}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ denote the set of compatible gradings on $\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})$ such that $S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}})$ , where $S$ is the set of edges with nonzero value in the grading. Given a grading $\omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\sh}_{d_{1},d_{2}}$ , define the grading $\theta(\omega)\coloneqq(\Omega(S_{\mathbf{E}}),\varphi_{\ell_{2}}^{*}S_{\mathbf{N}})$ on $\mathcal{D}_{\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}}$ as in [51, Section 4.2]. By definition, we have $\wt(\theta(\omega))=\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)$ . Then by [51, Lemma 4.4 and Proposition 4.20], we have

$$ \displaystyle x[\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}] \displaystyle=x_{1}^{-\ell_{2}d_{2}+d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{[\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1}]_{+},d_{2}}}\wt(\omega^{\prime})x_{1}^{\omega^{\prime}(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega^{\prime}(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})} \displaystyle=x_{1}^{-\ell_{2}d_{2}+d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}^{\sh}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}\wt(\theta(\omega))x_{1}^{\ell_{2}d_{2}-\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})} \displaystyle=x_{1}^{-\ell_{2}d_{2}+d_{1}}x_{2}^{-d_{2}}\sum_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}_{d_{1},d_{2}}}P_{2}(x_{2})^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})-d_{1}}\wt^{\prime\prime}(\omega)x_{1}^{\ell_{2}d_{2}-\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})}x_{2}^{\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})}. $$

Thus in all cases, we can conclude $\sigma_{2}(x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}])=x[\ell_{2}d_{2}-d_{1},d_{2}]$ . ∎

#### Corollary A.10 (following [51, Corollary 2.18]).

For any $(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ the generalized greedy element $x[d_{1},d_{2}]\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ defined by (3.19) is contained in $\mathcal{A}(P_{1},P_{2})$ .

#### Proof.

First note that $x^{\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]$ and $x^{\prime\prime}[d_{1},d_{2}]$ are contained in $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ for any $d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ . By definition, for any $z\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ , we have $\sigma_{1}(z)\in\mathcal{T}_{0}$ and $\sigma_{2}(z)\in\mathcal{T}_{2}$ . The result then follows directly from Theorem A.3 and Proposition A.9. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.18.

This can be proved in the same way as [51, Theorem 2.15], except with the above results replacing their more specialized analogues in [51]. In particular, we replace references to [51, Proposition 2.17] with Proposition A.9 and [51, Corollary 2.18] with Corollary A.10, and the remainder of the argument proceeds unchanged. ∎

## Appendix B Every wall coefficient in the Badlands is non-trivial

As a direct application of our results, we can prove that for any rank- $2$ generalized cluster scattering diagram, every wall-function coefficient of every wall in the Badlands is strictly positive. The Badlands of the scattering diagram $\mathfrak{D}\coloneqq\Scat(P_{1},P_{2})$ is the same region as the Badlands of $\mathfrak{D}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ .

The density of the Badlands in $\mathfrak{D}_{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}$ was suggested by various sources, including [27, Example 1.15], [29, Example 1.6], and [30, Example 1.4], before recently being proved by Gräfnitz and Luo [23]. In fact, Gräfnitz and Luo prove the stronger result that every wall-function coefficient of walls in the Badlands is strictly positive (except those that trivially vanish by the choice of $\ell_{1},\ell_{2}$ ). In the skew-symmetric case, density was proven in 2010 by Gross–Pandharipande [28] and strict positivity of every wall-function coefficient was proven in 2021 by Davison–Mandel [13]. All the previous approaches use either representation theory or deformations of scattering diagrams.
